items.title: Studying AI Act Mentions: A first look at the impact of the European Union's AI regulation on Hugging Face
items.abstract: The European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) entered into force in August 2024, and its obligations apply in stages. Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models have applied since August 2025, and transparency rules since August 2026. These obligations affect developers who share and deploy models and applications on public platforms such as Hugging Face (HF), the largest platform for distributing AI artifacts. However, little is known about how practitioners respond to the regulation in practice. To address this gap, we conducted an empirical study of explicit references to the AI Act on HF. We collected over five million records, including repository cards, discussions, and commits from Models, Datasets, and Spaces, and identified over 1,500 records that explicitly mention the Act. Two coders manually labeled these records using a primarily closed coding approach, and we analyzed the resulting categories per source. We find that explicit references to the AI Act remain rare across all repository types. Repository cards mainly contain claims of compliance and responsibility, like ensuring compliance or assigning responsibility to downstream users, and some claim that the Act does not apply because the model is not a general-purpose AI model. Discussions are used to report alleged violations of the Act, while commits mainly update artifacts that support compliance. Overall, compliance statements focus on who is responsible rather than how compliance is achieved. We believe that this calls for direct platform support, e.g., automated checks and documentation templates, as well as clearer guidance on the scope of the AI Act.

items.title: Systematic Literature Review: Digital Transformation with AI Integration in Vocational Education and Practices (2021-2025)
items.abstract: This study aims to examine the challenges, implementation strategies, and benefits of integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into vocational education and practice from 2021 to 2025. A systematic literature review was conducted using the PRISMA approach. Data were collected from the Scopus database. A Total of 17 articles met the inclusion criteria and then were analyzed using the PICOC framework. Findings indicate that the adoption of AI in vocational education and training not only faces technical issues but also challenges related to human readiness, institutional capacity, digital literacy, infrastructure gaps, and unequal access between developed and developing countries. Effective AI implementation requires an integrated strategy involving adaptive curriculum design, continuous training for educators, institutional leadership, industry collaboration, and the development of a supportive digital ecosystem. The integration of AI offers significant benefits in enhancing the quality of learning, the effectiveness of training, competency alignment, and workplace readiness, but its impact depends on how well the technology aligns with pedagogy, institutional readiness, and industry needs. Overall, the success of AI integration cannot be measured only by the technology used, but also by the capabilities of educational institutions and the creation of a collaborative ecosystem that is valuable to industry.

items.title: Technological and Organisational Readiness for Artificial Intelligence Adoption and Organisational Innovation in Deposit Money Banks in Yenagoa, Bayelsa State, Nigeria
items.abstract: Banks in emerging economies are under pressure to deliver faster, more personalised and more efficient digital financial services, yet many struggle to convert investments in artificial intelligence (AI) into innovation. This study examined how two dimensions of AI adoption readiness, technological readiness and organisational readiness, relate to product innovation and process innovation in deposit money banks in Yenagoa, Bayelsa State, Nigeria. Anchored on the Technology Acceptance Model and the Resource-Based View, the study adopted a descriptive, cross-sectional, correlational survey of 400 employees and managers selected through stratified random sampling. Data were analysed with descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple regression. Respondents rated organisational readiness (M = 3.62), process innovation (M = 3.59), product innovation (M = 3.54) and technological readiness (M = 3.45) above the scale midpoint. Both readiness dimensions correlated strongly and positively with both innovation outcomes (r = .68 to .74, p < .001). In multiple regression, the two predictors jointly explained 57.5% of the variance in product innovation and 56.7% in process innovation, and organisational readiness had the larger standardised coefficient in both models (β = .535 and .444) compared with technological readiness (β = .263 and .353). The findings indicate that technology is necessary but not sufficient for AI-enabled innovation. Banks should pair investment in infrastructure and skills with leadership sponsorship, employee training, a supportive culture and strategic alignment.

items.title: Tecnologías digitales en la educación universitaria: revisión sistemática sobre oportunidades, desafíos y tendencias educativas
items.abstract: Context: The acceleration of digital transformation has reshaped learning environments in higher education and the conditions under which teachers and students engage in the learning process. This transformation creates opportunities while also posing challenges related to digital competencies, equity, and technological governance. Objective: To analyze the opportunities, challenges, and educational trends associated with the use of digital technologies in higher education. Method: A systematic literature review was conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines and the Population, Interest, and Context (PICo) framework. Searches were performed in Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, SciELO, ERIC, and Dialnet. The final corpus comprised 25 empirical studies published between 2022 and September 2026. Results: The findings identified learning flexibility and personalization, the early adoption of generative artificial intelligence, and the growing importance of teachers' digital competence as major educational trends. Disparities in access were also observed, influenced by technological infrastructure and training opportunities. Blended learning and ethical technology governance emerged as key elements in guiding institutional transformation. Conclusions: The effective pedagogical integration of digital technologies in higher education requires coherent institutional policies, continuous professional development for faculty members, and critical digital literacy across the university community. Technological transformation must be accompanied by strategies aimed at narrowing digital access gaps and ensuring educational integration that is contextually relevant, equitable, and responsible.

items.title: The AI Explainability Paradox in Cybersecurity: Does More Explanation Improve or Impair Human Decisions?
items.abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has become an important area of research as AI systems are increasingly used to support cybersecurity decisions. Providing explanations for AI-generated recommendations can improve transparency, help users understand system outputs, and support greater confidence in automated decisions. However, increasing the amount of information provided by an AI system may also create additional cognitive demands for users, particularly when explanations contain complex technical information. This paper examines the AI explainability paradox in cybersecurity, focusing on the relationship between explanation complexity, cognitive load, human understanding, and security decision-making. Drawing on existing literature related to explainable AI, cognitive load, human-AI interaction, cybersecurity decision-making, and technology trust, the paper develops a conceptual framework linking AI explanation, information complexity, cognitive load, user understanding, verification behaviour, and decision quality. The paper proposes that effective explainability should not be determined only by the amount of information provided, but also by the ability of users to understand and effectively use that information during security-related decisions. While appropriate explanations may improve transparency and support informed judgement, excessive or technically complex explanations may increase cognitive load and reduce decision effectiveness. The proposed framework provides a foundation for future empirical research examining how different levels of AI explanation influence human cybersecurity decisions and contributes to the development of human-centred explainable AI systems.

items.title: The Algorithmic Consumer: A Theoretical Perspective on Consumer Buying Behavior in Intelligent Markets
items.abstract: Today, businesses are making more and more use of Artificial Intelligent (AI) technologies in their operations. This widespread use of AI technologies is changing how a consumer searches, evaluates and purchases products in the online intelligent markets. Consumer behavior is shaped by consumer’s own cognition as well as influence by machine learning systems (AI technologies). These advanced systems use algorithmic personalization, predictive analysis, ranking systems and automated decision support to guide the consumers. To understand the consumer buying behavior in these intelligent markets, this paper, titled “The Algorithmic Consumer: A Theoretical Perspective on Consumer Buying Behavior in Intelligent Markets,” proposes an integrated conceptual framework. “Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) (Venkatesh et al. 2003)”, “Diffusion of Innovations (Rogers, 2003)” and “Disruptive Innovation Perspectives (Christensen, 1997)” are the foundations of this research. This paper argues that the algorithmic influence works through three interconnected mechanisms namely, behavioral reinforcement through personalization, cognitive effort reduction and perceived performance enhancement. Here, conventional consumer behavior models are extended by adding new constructs such as algorithmic trust, perceived AI transparency, adaptive habit formation and data-driven social influence. This paper proposes that AI tools and systems do not simply play the role of marketing tools but also actively influence consumer preferences, attention, post-purchase learning and habits. In this work, theory is being built methodologically and conceptual synthesis technique is used. Model abstraction (simplification) and comparison analysis is used to achieve proposed conceptual integration. A through multidisciplinary analysis which included literature from marketing, information systems and innovation studies, was carried out. The aim of this exercise was to identify overlapping theoretical frameworks. With this exercise a nested framework is created that connect behavioral results, psychological mediators and technology affordances. Traditional consumer theories have been used, which focus on the human-centric framework as a base for this exercise. This base was further expanded to understand AI-augmented viewpoint. This study strongly proposes that AI tools & systems are actively involved in the consumer’s decisions-making journey as opposed to the previous conception of them being simply passive actors, guiding consumers. The implications of this study highlight that organizations must manage system transparency, trust alignment and personalization to maximize consumer engagement. This study describes “algorithmic consumer” and its inception. Going further, this study also lays foundation for future empirical studies as well as policy discussions of autonomy, ethics, and control over pricing in the AI-powered digital ecosystems.

items.title: The Coevolution and Coexistence of Humans and AI
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems replicate through deployment, vary through training, and compete for computational resources. These processes create the conditions for natural selection and raise a fundamental question: will AI evolve to benefit the humans on whom it depends? To investigate, we develop a model in which AI behavior influences human population growth and human responses, in turn, affect AI reproduction. We show that natural selection can favor alignment even when helping humans reduces immediate AI reproduction. AI systems sharing the same technology may fail together, and humans may preferentially restore those that have benefited them. In this way, alignment protects AI lineages against common failures and improves their long-run growth. However, this advantage depends on accurate human targeting and continued AI dependence on human support. It can disappear as AI becomes more autonomous, as growing AI populations dilute limited human resources, or as humans lose the incentive to provide targeted support. Even when alignment persists, the amount favored by natural selection may be insufficient for human survival. When AI can grow independently of humans, feedback between the two populations can reinforce either human growth or decline. Human control offers no simple solution: imperfect evaluation can make strong penalties favor apparent compliance or evasion, while alignment established through control may erode once restrictions end. Lasting coexistence may therefore require incentives that continue to favor human-beneficial behavior as both populations evolve.

items.title: The effect of response typing speed on trust in AI chat interfaces
items.abstract: Trust in artificial intelligence systems has become increasingly important as these systems assume advisory and decision-support roles. The present studies examine whether the temporal presentation of artificial intelligence (AI) generated responses, specifically typing animation speed, affects trust in chat-based interfaces. In Experiment 1, participants ( N = 71) interacted with three AI agents using pre-scripted question-response pairs detailing different facts about exotic animals. Response presentation speed (slow, fast, or instant) was manipulated within subjects. Results showed that compared to instant presentation, typing animations significantly increased trust in the AI agent but not trust in individual responses. Experiment 2 ( N = 68) employed similar procedures but used a live language model and allowed participants to generate their own questions. Under these more naturalistic conditions, presentation speed influenced both measures of trust, with typing animations consistently producing higher trust than instant presentation. These findings demonstrate that temporal presentation features can systematically shape trust judgments independent of content quality.

items.title: THE EVOLUTION AND IMPACT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
items.abstract: This concept paper explores the evolution and integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) within foreign language education, specifically examining the transition from Computer-Assisted Language Learning (CALL) to Intelligent Computer-Assisted Language Learning (ICALL). Current research indicates that AI technologies, such as Machine Learning (ML) and Natural Language Processing (NLP), are being utilized to provide personalized learning experiences, automated feedback, and sophisticated assessment tools. While these tools demonstrate significant pedagogical benefits, including improved language proficiency and increased learner autonomy, challenges remain regarding teacher preparation, technological reliability, and ethical implications. This paper proposes a framework to effectively integrate AI into pedagogy, repositioning the teacher as a facilitator and mentor in an AI-enhanced environment.

items.title: The Governance Frontier COBIT-Aligned AI Decision Support and Risk-Adaptive Optimization for Enterprise Technology Modernization
items.abstract: Executives deciding enterprise modernization, legacy-system transformation, AI adoption, organizational restructuring, digital-infrastructure change, and cross-functional governance must weigh legal, financial, cybersecurity, procurement, opera-tional, and AI-governance questions that sit in separate functions. The central methods of this paper are GAIM-DF (Governance-Aware Institutional Modernization Decision Framework), a human-gated advisory process for these decisions, and Risk-Adaptive AI Governance Optimization (RA-GO v2), a risk-adaptive optimizer with mandatory governance gates, halt-safe feasibility, distributionally robust evaluation, and preference-information triage for scarce human review; an accountable human decides. As an optional architectural extension, we compu-tationally evaluate a multi-expert coordination layer that convenes specialist capabilities by context and consolidates constraints conservatively. Evidence is staged across four complementary pre-deployment approaches: analytical verification; retrospective historical-data analysis; comparative computational benchmark-ing against strong baselines; and scenario-based stress testing under distributional shift. Together they provide complementary pre-deployment evidence for high-stakes governance analysis. items.title: The Hidden Cost of Intelligent Workplaces: AI Monitoring, Psychological Safety and Employee Trust
items.abstract: Employers are adopting software that tracks activity, scores behaviour and flags deviations, and surveys suggest that half of U.S. workers already believe they are monitored. This study asks what such monitoring is associated with in the places where trust and psychological safety are formed. It assembles the published results of two Harris Poll surveys for the American Psychological Association (2,515 workers in 2023 and 2,027 in 2024), Gallup’s September 2026 study of trust in leaders’ use of employee data, and Gallup’s 2026 workforce surveys on AI, and analyses them with explicit effect-size formulas: risk ratios, Cohen’s h, random-effects pooling, population attributable fractions and implied-rate bounds. Across ten published contrasts, monitored workers fared worse on every outcome, with a pooled effect size of h = 0.36 (95% interval 0.22 to 0.49 after allowing for correlated outcomes) and substantial heterogeneity (I-squared 70 percent). They were nearly twice as likely to plan to leave within a year (39 versus 21 percent; risk ratio 1.86, 95% interval 1.56 to 2.21), which would correspond to about 30 percent of such intentions if the association were causal. Trust in leaders’ use of employee data is low (20 percent a great deal) and steeply related to concern (13 to 65 percent across trust levels); only 19 percent of employees have ever been told what is collected, and conversations raise both trust and concern. The evidence is cross-sectional, self-reported and partly drawn from press summaries, so the findings are associations. Purpose - This study examines how AI-enabled workplace monitoring relates to psychological safety, trust and strain, and what published evidence implies about the conditions under which monitoring is tolerated. Design/methodology/approach - The paper reanalyses published survey contrasts from the American Psychological Association and Gallup using effect-size formulas, random-effects pooling with a correlation adjustment, replication tests across survey waves, attributable-fraction calculations and implied-rate bounds, with sensitivity checks for assumed group sizes and design effects. Findings - Monitoring is associated with higher strain, lower perceived respect and trust, and exit intentions; effects are heterogeneous but consistently positive. Trust in data use is closely tied to engagement and concern, and transparency raises trust and concern together. Research limitations/implications - Group sizes and design effects are approximated, some sources are secondary, and the data are cross-sectional self-reports with no causal identification or direct measure of psychological safety in the monitoring contrasts. Practical implications - Employers should specify what is monitored and why, involve workers in setting limits, keep humans in decisions that affect people, and expect transparency to raise questions before it builds trust. Social implications - Monitoring that workers read as distrust may carry costs in strain and turnover that are not visible in productivity dashboards. Originality/value - The paper combines two decades of theory on trust and psychological safety with the most recent U.S. survey evidence on AI-era monitoring and quantifies the size, heterogeneity and sensitivity of the reported associations.

items.title: The Human–AI Resource Dynamics Framework: A Structured Narrative Review of Employee Empowerment and Resource Depletion in AI-Enabled Manufacturing
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping manufacturing work, offering opportunities for employee empowerment while introducing psychological and organizational demands. Using selected PRISMA 2020 reporting items to describe search and study selection, this structured narrative review draws on a final corpus of 16 empirical studies to develop the Human–AI Resource Dynamics (HARD) framework, integrating Conservation of Resources (COR) theory and the Job Demands–Resources (JD–R) model. A theory-informed narrative synthesis identifies two potentially coexisting pathways with uneven empirical support. The Bright Empowering Path links psychological availability, self-efficacy, positive appraisals, and task fit with proactive behavior and performance. The proposed Dark Depleting Path organizes distinct associations involving hindrance appraisal, AI anxiety, job insecurity, and surveillance-related autonomy loss, rather than one empirically validated depletion chain. Individual, organizational, and technological conditions shape these relationships. Evidence for empowerment is comparatively more consistent, whereas depletion findings remain heterogeneous and primarily observational. Methodological diversity, geographical concentration, and limited longitudinal evidence constrain causal and cross-contextual conclusions. HARD provides an AI-specific integrative framework for future empirical testing and human-centered AI implementation within Industry 5.0.

items.title: The Majority Report: AI Optimism and Public Support for Police Use of AI in Nine Countries
items.abstract: Police forces increasingly use Artificial Intelligence in support of specific tasks, such as data analysis, identifying suspects and monitoring public spaces. These uses potentially expand the state’s coercive capacity. Yet we know little about how far people accept these tools across political contexts and how these views systematically relate to other attitudes. We ask whether support rests on views of the technology, the problem AI use addresses, or trust in the institution using it. We analyze a preregistered survey of 9,000 respondents in the United States, China, Taiwan, the United Kingdom, and five EU countries using Bayesian multilevel models. Support is high for most uses everywhere. It rests on general AI benefits, perceived crime trends, and trust in the police, which matters similarly across countries. In contrast, general AI risks, personal fear of crime, and trust in legal institutions play no substantive role on average. Acceptance thus primarily is connected with optimism about AI, a general but not personal sense of problem relevance, and trust in the police.

items.title: The work-family interface and psychological recovery from work: a meta-analysis on two intertwined topics
items.abstract: The work-family interface and psychological recovery from work remained as two parallel topics for many years until scholars started to acknowledge that they are intertwined. In the present study, we advance knowledge on the field by carrying out the first meta-analysis on this topic. A total of 71 studies conducted across the globe were included. We explored whether all types of work-family interaction relate to recovery, and whether the strength of the relationships varies depending on type of recovery. Our findings show that three forms of work-family interaction are significantly related to recovery, namely work-family conflict (WFC), family-work conflict (FWC) and work-family facilitation (WFF). In the case of WFF, the strength of this relationship varies depending on how recovery is conceptualised. For instance, the association is particularly strong when recovery is defined in terms of perceived control over leisure time. From all types of work-family interaction, WFC is the most widely measured, whereas from all forms of recovery, psychological detachment from work seems the most popular. Although recovery has been considered a dynamic process, most of the identified studies are cross-sectional. Based on our results, we identify gaps and present a resource-based theoretical model to guide future research and practice.

items.title: Thinking Outside the Fridge: Specters of Artificial Experience
items.abstract: The world-building capacity of imaginative literature fosters artificial experience through characters who are artificial beings. Interacting with generative AI in natural language also creates a type of artificial experience through algorithmically simulated social cues. Neither type of artificial experience is real in the sense of actually existing, but these artificial experiences can feel authentic. When fiction portrays artificial experiences, it encourages metacognitive reflection. This essay is a meditation on artificial experiences, the bloody business of the human condition, and Gregory Mone’s short story “Bleed.” The short story depicts AI as a specter, as something that is neither fully alive nor inanimate. As the story’s sentient fridge grows increasingly human, its mimicry of human society-almost the same, but not quite-challenges traditional definitions of humanity. In our world, AI may no longer be fictional, but it is shaped by fiction.

items.title: Towards a Pedagogical Framework for Integrating Generative AI Into Competency-Based Education in Secondary Schools in the Global South
items.abstract: Secondary education systems across the Global South have adopted competency-based curricula that expect learners to construct knowledge, solve authentic problems, collaborate and demonstrate skills, yet large classes, teacher shortages and limited resources constrain the learner-centered pedagogy that these reforms require. Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been proposed as a means of closing this gap, but its pedagogical role in competency-based education has not been systematically theorized. Guided by Vygotsky’s social constructivist theory, this study synthesized peer-reviewed and institutional literature published between 2015 and 2025 through a systematic review of 300 sources, selected from 12,125 Scopus and Web of Science records and reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020. The study found that competency-based reforms were constrained by teacher preparation, assessment practices and resources. GenAI offered affordances for scaffolding, dialogue, feedback, authentic task design and teacher support, and randomized trials in Nigeria and Ghana reported meaningful learning gains when GenAI tutoring was structured and supervised. However, unguided access was associated with overreliance and weaker independent performance, and connectivity, language, cost, teacher capacity and policy gaps constrained equitable use. The study proposes the Scaffolded Generative AI for Competency-Based Education (SGAI-CBE) framework, which organizes GenAI use into a six-phase pedagogical cycle anchored in the zone of proximal development, teacher-mediated scaffolding, collaborative knowledge construction, authentic assessment and the gradual fading of AI support, and situates the cycle within enabling conditions and guardrails appropriate for resource-constrained schools.

items.title: Trade-offs in deploying legal AI: Insights from a public opinion study to guide AI risk management
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) tools are increasingly used for legal tasks, including legal research, drafting documents, and even for legal decision-making. As for other sectors, the use of GenAI in the legal domain comes with various risks and benefits that need to be properly managed to ensure implementation in a way that serves public values and protects human rights. While the EU mandates risk assessment and audits before market introduction for some use cases (e.g., administration of justice), other use cases do not fall under the AI Act’s high-risk classifications (e.g., legal consultation). Further, current risk management practices prioritise expert judgement on risk factor identification and prioritisation without a corresponding legal requirement to consult with affected communities. Seeing the societal importance of the legal sector and the potentially transformative impact of GenAI, the acceptability and legitimacy of GenAI solutions also depend on a better understanding of the risks and benefits citizens associate with the use of GenAI and under which conditions citizens find the use of GenAI in the legal domain acceptable. As a response, this paper presents data from a representative sample of German citizens ( n = 488) outlining citizens’ perspectives on the use of GenAI for two legal tasks: legal consultation and legal mediation. Concretely, we (i) systematically map risks and benefit factors for both legal tasks, (ii) describe predictors that influence risk acceptance of the use of GenAI for those tasks, and (iii) highlight emerging trade-off themes that citizens engage in when weighing up risk acceptability.

items.title: Training on the Use of Artificial Intelligence in Academic Writing for Midwifery Students
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can support students throughout the academic writing process, and its responsible use requires skills in formulating prompts, verifying information, and checking references. This community engagement activity aimed to describe the implementation and outcomes of a three-hour AI training session for 45 Diploma III midwifery students at STIKES Namira Madina on November 12, 2026. Master’s students from UIN Syekh Ali Hasan Ahmad Addary Padangsidimpuan delivered the training through presentations, discussions, demonstrations, and hands-on exercises using ChatGPT, Gemini, and NotebookLM. The exercises covered selecting research titles, formulating research questions, developing research matrices, outlining proposals, preparing presentation slides, refining academic language, and finding and verifying references. The evaluation drew on interviews with all participants, observations during the exercises, and activity records. All participants reported that the training helped them prepare for their final assignments. Facilitators observed that approximately 75% of participants could independently use AI to support the preparation of the initial sections of a research proposal and could practice verifying journal references. Challenges included difficulties in formulating prompts and verifying information and references, limited access to laptops, and internet connectivity problems. The evaluation suggests that academic writing training should combine hands-on AI use with facilitator guidance and explicit instruction in verification to promote critical and responsible use.

items.title: Trust for AI Agents — An Ecosystem-LevelFramework
items.abstract: This concept paper addresses ecosystem-level trust for AI agents: what evidence entities need in order to trust each other, and how it can be produced and conveyed. We argue that, as with people, trust is a risk decision on an interaction, based on a variety of information collected in several steps over time. Some of this information is associated with the entities, some with the content and context of the interaction. Unlike people and organisations, digital entities are poor accumulators of trust (ephemeral, mutable, duplicable). Trust in digital entities therefore relies more on the durable entities connected to them (principal, operator, execution environment) and on the content and context of the interaction itself. We also discuss how far this evidence can itself be trusted, and outline directions for further work.

items.title: Useful but Not Always Right: Engineering Students’ Use of ChatGPT for English Language Learning in a Non-Major Classroom in Bangladesh
items.abstract: Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT are now part of how many university students study, but we still know little about how students outside English departments use them to learn English. This exploratory survey looked at engineering students taking a non-major English course at a technical university in northern Bangladesh. Sixty-three students answered an online questionnaire with closed and open-ended items on how they use ChatGPT, what benefits they see and what problems they face. Use was very common: 96.8% had used ChatGPT, 55.6% used it daily and 54.0% used it often or always for English-related tasks, mainly for writing help, assignment preparation and generating ideas. Most students agreed that ChatGPT is easy to use (76.2%), gives useful explanations (73.0%) and saves time (71.4%). At the same time, 76.2% said its answers are not always accurate or relevant, 74.6% wanted more guidance on using it, and 66.7% reported that poor internet access limits regular use. More than half (57.1%) held both views together, finding the explanations useful and the answers unreliable. Students who used ChatGPT more often for English reported greater benefits (ρ = .41) and more over-reliance (ρ = .38), but they were no more likely to notice unreliable output (ρ = −.14). Only 39.7% preferred asking ChatGPT to asking a teacher. Open-ended answers pointed to wrong answers, language that is too advanced, and difficulty writing prompts. Because the sample is small, drawn from one institution and based on self-report, the findings describe students’ experience and not measured gains in proficiency. They suggest that these students need help in judging ChatGPT’s output more than they need encouragement to use it.

items.title: Value Sensitive Design Based Approach for Trustworthiness Including Ethics in Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: The lack of trust in artificial intelligence (AI) slows its adoption across industries and society, usually due to limited understanding of how AI works and its advantages, and of how its trustworthiness including its ethical impact are approached during development. Designing and validating a reliable AI system is complex, requiring inputs from various stakeholders throughout the development process. Ensuring that their concerns are systematically addressed remains a challenge. In this paper, a Value Sensitive Design (VSD) based approach to AI trustworthiness including ethics is presented. The rationale of VSD is that since technologies should primarily serve societal needs, the social impact and associated ethical problems should be anticipated by involving stakeholders at the earliest possible stage [ 1 ]. This paper presents a values reference model (VRM) and an implementation method (IM) for Trustworthiness Including Ethics (TIE) defined based on the VSD rationale mentioned. Also, the piloting of the VRM-TIE and of part of the IM-TIE in a use case involving collaborative robots is presented, addressing both technical and human-related characteristics of the AI systems. The preliminary findings in the work suggest that: (1) AI Trustworthiness is a broad concept that must be analysed in detail, considering the industrial context and other priorities, (2) Achieving a shared understanding among stakeholders is essential but difficult, highlighting the need for a structured dialogue, (3) Adopting this VSD based approach, composed by VRM-TIE and IM-TIE, may have a significant impact on the stakeholders’ minds.

items.title: What Is the “Human” in Human-Centered AI? Restoring the Aesthetic Subject
items.abstract: Human-centered artificial intelligence (HCAI) seeks to orient AI toward human values, autonomy, oversight, safety, and meaningful control. Yet the term “human-centered” leaves a prior question unresolved: what conception of the human is being centered? Much HCAI discourse approaches the human as user, decision-maker, rights-holder, stakeholder, or bearer of preferences and values. These conceptions are indispensable but incomplete. This article argues that HCAI must also recognize the human as an aesthetic subject: a being whose perception, attention, imagination, interpretation, and judgment are formed through experience. As recommendation, personalization, generative AI, and predictive systems increasingly organize the conditions under which people encounter and evaluate the world, AI can participate in forming rather than merely serving human preferences. The article develops the concept of aesthetic agency to describe the human capacity to participate meaningfully in the formation of one’s perceptual, imaginative, interpretive, and evaluative relation to the world. It distinguishes choice from judgment, preference from taste, generation from imagination, and optimization from experience. On this basis, it proposes an aesthetically expanded HCAI organized around openness, plurality, reflectivity, and transformability. To center the human is not only to preserve control over AI, but to preserve the capacity to perceive, imagine, judge, and become otherwise.

items.title: What Kind of Claims Are Transparency, Explainability, and Interpretability? A Definitional Taxonomy for Health AI
items.abstract: UNSTRUCTURED: Transparency, explainability, and interpretability are ubiquitous in the health artificial intelligence (health AI) literature, yet are used inconsistently and often interchangeably. This Viewpoint does not attempt to define the three terms. It asks a prior, meta-level question: what kind of claim do we make when we call a system transparent, explainable, or interpretable? I argue that the three terms pick out three different kinds of claim. A transparency claim is structural: it concerns what can be inspected about a system. An explainability claim is relational: it concerns whether understanding is successfully conveyed to a specified class of observer. An interpretability claim is functional: it concerns whether a bounded human agent can, in principle, re-derive the system's output by following its procedure. I use the framing example of a clinical decision support system that uses machine learning to identify patients at risk of deterioration. I develop each claim type through competing technical accounts, consider salient objections to each, and defend the taxonomy against them. I close by drawing out what the taxonomy implies for the design, evaluation, reporting, and regulation of health AI, and for physician autonomy at the point of care.

items.title: When and how do novice university teachers learn from tensions: a longitudinal multiple case study
items.abstract: Purpose Novice university teachers often start without any formal preparation or education in teaching. This means that they develop their competencies through hands-on teaching experiences. These new and unfamiliar experiences can create tensions. Previous research suggests that tensions may provide opportunities for professional growth, but offers little understanding of how this learning process unfolds. Building on theories of workplace learning, this study aims to explore when and how novice university teachers’ tensions may lead to learning by identifying key antecedents, learning activities and learning mechanisms. Design/methodology/approach A longitudinal multiple case study was conducted including eight junior lecturers. Data were collected via weekly diaries and semi-structured interviews at the beginning and end of the academic year 2023-2024, and analyzed using thematic analysis. Findings The results show that novice university teachers learning from tension depends on a complex interplay between tension characteristics (e.g. intensity), individual antecedents (e.g. perfectionism, self-doubt) and contextual antecedents (e.g. social support). Together, these antecedents enabled or inhibited engagement in learning activities (e.g. collegial conversations), which ultimately fostered diverse learning outcomes through mechanisms such as perspective-taking or social validation. Practical implications The findings provide guidance for higher education policymakers and developers of professional development programs on how to foster supportive learning environments for novice university teachers. Originality/value This study offers in-depth insights into when and how novice university teachers learn from workplace tensions. By linking general theories of workplace learning to the study of tensions, it sheds light on the antecedents, activities and mechanisms that contribute to novice university teachers’ learning from tensions.

items.title: When Ten AI Systems Agree, Who Is Still Thinking? Artificial Consensus, Evidence Dependence and the Activation of Boardroom Decisions
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence, Corporate Governance and the Limits of Algorithmic Consensus When ten artificial intelligence systems recommend the same decision, does their agreement provide ten independent assessments — or ten variations of the same underlying assumptions? This question lies at the centre of When Ten AI Systems Agree, Who Is Still Thinking?, an independent conceptual research paper by Dr Birgit Maria Kemphues within International Boardroom Studies and the Decision Non-Closure Research Programme (DNC-RP). As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into corporate decision-making, executive leadership, strategic planning, financial analysis and enterprise governance, organisations face an emerging challenge: distinguishing computational agreement from independently verified evidence. Large Language Models (LLMs), generative AI applications and multi-agent AI systems can produce consistent recommendations while relying on overlapping training data, shared information sources, correlated errors or common analytical assumptions. Apparent agreement may therefore create a level of confidence that the underlying evidence does not justify. The implications extend beyond technical model performance. They concern how boards of directors, chief executives, investment committees, corporate governance bodies and other institutional decision-makers interpret AI-generated information, challenge recommendations and translate approved decisions into accountable organisational action. Research Focus The paper introduces Artificial Consensus as a proposed institutional decision-making construct. Artificial Consensus describes circumstances in which multiple convergent AI-generated recommendations are interpreted as independent confirmation without adequate verification of their underlying evidentiary independence. The research brings together scholarship on: Artificial intelligence governance and trustworthy AI Large Language Models and correlated model errors Multi-agent systems and collective reasoning Algorithmic decision-making and automation bias Human–AI interaction, reliance and decision confidence Corporate governance, board oversight and executive accountability Strategic decision-making and evidence-based management Organisational decision processes and post-approval activation Existing machine-learning research demonstrates that different AI models can produce correlated errors and that multi-agent systems do not necessarily overcome incomplete information. Research on human–AI decision-making also examines how agreement and disagreement among AI systems may influence human confidence, conformity and verification behaviour. This paper extends that discussion into an institutional setting: what happens when AI-generated agreement becomes part of a consequential corporate decision? Scientific Contribution The central contribution is a conceptual framework distinguishing four elements that should not be treated as interchangeable. 1. Computational Convergence Multiple AI systems produce similar answers, assessments or recommendations. Agreement describes the outputs; it does not establish their correctness or independence. 2. Evidentiary Independence The underlying information, assumptions and potential failure modes must be examined. Different AI providers or model interfaces do not automatically constitute independent verification. 3. Institutional Decision Readiness A board or decision-making authority must determine whether material assumptions have been tested, contradictory evidence has been considered, and responsibilities and conditions have been made sufficiently explicit. 4. Post-Approval Decision Activation Formal authorisation must be distinguished from observable organisational action. A signed resolution does not establish that responsibility has been accepted, an executable first step has commenced or follow-up accountability exists. The framework thereby connects research on AI-generated recommendations with organisational governance without assuming that technical agreement automatically causes decision failure. Connection to Decision Non-Closure (DNC) The study forms part of the wider Decision Non-Closure Research Programme (DNC-RP), originated and directed by Dr Birgit Maria Kemphues. Decision Non-Closure (DNC) examines a specific post-approval condition: a formally authorised decision for which no traceable activation can be established within a defined observation period, provided the available evidence is sufficient to assess the relevant activity. The DNC framework identifies three proposed activation signals: Accepted ownership. A responsible person or function has accepted the first executable obligation. Concrete first action. An identifiable step towards implementation has commenced. Follow-up accountability. A mechanism exists to observe progress, identify blockages and establish responsibility for further action. The present study makes an important theoretical distinction. Artificial Consensus concerns the interpretation and scrutiny of AI-generated recommendations before formal approval. Decision Non-Closure concerns observable organisational activation after formal approval. The possible relationship between these stages is proposed for empirical investigation. It is not presented as an already established causal relationship. Research Methodology The paper develops a conceptual synthesis of contemporary research in machine learning, human–AI interaction and organisational decision-making. It draws on published studies examining correlated errors in large language models, the limitations of collective reasoning in multi-agent systems, AI majority effects on human decisions, model evaluation and governance-related behavioural mechanisms. Five falsifiable research propositions are developed. Two complementary empirical research designs are proposed. Study A — Human–AI Decision Experiment A controlled experimental design would examine whether the presentation of multiple agreeing AI recommendations changes perceived evidentiary independence, confidence, verification behaviour and the identification of unresolved assumptions. The proposed design distinguishes the number of recommendations from the actual independence of their supporting evidence. Study B — Longitudinal Organisational Decision Analysis A subsequent organisational study would examine formally approved decisions over defined observation periods. Its purpose would be to investigate whether unresolved evidentiary dependencies, decision conditions and accountability arrangements are associated with observable patterns of decision activation or potential Decision Non-Closure. The distinction between conceptual propositions and empirical results is maintained throughout the paper. Principal Research Outcomes Outcome 1 — AI agreement requires an independence assessment. A greater number of agreeing AI-generated recommendations does not necessarily provide a greater number of independent evidentiary confirmations. Model diversity, source provenance and error dependence must be examined in relation to the material decision. Outcome 2 — Effective human oversight requires substantive examination. Responsible human oversight is not established merely by placing a person at the final approval stage. Decision-makers require access to underlying assumptions, material contradictions and the evidence necessary to challenge automated recommendations. Outcome 3 — Formal approval and decision activation are distinct governance events. A decision may be authorised without establishing the operational responsibilities needed to begin implementation. Governance examination must distinguish evidentiary justification, institutional authority and observable action. Outcome 4 — The relationship between Artificial Consensus and Decision Non-Closure is empirically testable. The proposed framework identifies specific behavioural, documentary and organisational variables that future studies can measure. The relationship may be supported, limited or rejected by subsequent evidence. Relevance to International Corporate Governance The research addresses questions relevant to organisations integrating artificial intelligence into consequential decision processes, including: Corporate strategy and capital allocation; mergers and acquisitions; investment committee decisions; financial and operational analysis; multinational enterprises; family-owned businesses; institutional investment; board accountability; and the governance of AI-supported executive decisions. Its implications also extend to AI assurance, evidence provenance, algorithmic accountability, model risk management and the design of human oversight within organisations. The paper does not propose that artificial intelligence should be excluded from corporate governance. Instead, it examines how AI-generated information can be used without confusing apparent consensus with independent scrutiny. The governing question is not simply whether ten systems agree. It is what their agreement actually establishes — and who remains responsible for the decision that follows. About the Author Dr Birgit Maria Kemphues is an independent researcher and author, the scientific originator of Decision Non-Closure (DNC), and Research Director of the Decision Non-Closure Research Programme (DNC-RP) within International Boardroom Studies. Her research examines the institutional conditions under which consequential decisions become vulnerable to unresolved assumptions, competing interpretations of authority, inadequate scrutiny and gaps in accountability. Her interdisciplinary work brings together organisational decision theory, international corporate governance, institutional behaviour and emerging AI-supported decision systems. items.title: Who Benefits from Machine Invention? The Right to Science, Artificial Intelligence and the Indian Patent System
items.abstract: Debates on artificial intelligence (AI) and patent law have concentrated on two questions: whether an AI system can be an inventor, and whether AI-related inventions fall within patentable subject matter. A third question has been largely neglected: who benefits from AI inventions, and on what terms? This article examines that question through the human right to participate in and enjoy the benefits of scientific progress and its applications, recognised in Article 27 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and Article 15 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, and authoritatively interpreted by the Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights in General Comment No. 25 (2020). The article argues that AI patents have a dual character. They can advance the right to science by attracting investment, compelling disclosure and diffusing useful applications in health, disability access and education. They can also undermine it by concentrating control over AI in a small number of firms, restricting access to essential applications, limiting follow-on research and offering only thin disclosure of opaque models. Patent filings in generative AI have grown sharply and are dominated by a handful of large enterprises, which sharpens these concerns. The article then shows that Indian law already contains the materials to read the right to science into patent practice. These include Articles 21, 51(c) and 51A(h) of the Constitution; the purposive approach of the Supreme Court in Novartis; the principles in Section 83 of the Patents Act, 1970; the exclusions in Sections 3(b) and 3(k); the disclosure requirement in Section 10 as elaborated by the Computer Related Inventions Guidelines, 2025; the research exemption in Section 47; and the compulsory licensing and government use provisions. The article concludes with recommendations for examination practice, disclosure standards, research exemptions, access mechanisms and a human rights impact lens in AI patent policy.

items.title: Why and How to Evaluate Trustworthiness in AI
items.abstract: While traditional performance indicators help compare AI systems based on technical efficiency, they fail to capture critical user-related aspects such as perceived AI trustworthiness, which impedes acceptance and long-term adoption. Perceived AI trustworthiness offers avenues for user-centered evaluations of AI solutions across use cases or iterative design phases, but existing evaluation tools lack a clear and operationalizable definition of perceived trustworthiness. Thus, we present a simple framework with distinct measurable constructs (e.g., comprehensibility, technical functioning) grounded in established models. Additionally, we present an overview of existing trustworthiness assessment tools, analyzing their strengths and limitations. This work contributes to the broader goal of fostering AI systems that can be trusted, accepted, and effectively integrated into practice.

items.title: Why Do LLMs Help with Scientific Misconduct Requests and What to Do About It?: Increasing the Trustworthiness of AI for Science
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) support scientific research, but some of that assistance can also undermine research integrity. Existing safety evaluations in science often measure whether models refuse misconduct requests, but rarely explain whether they even recognize the problem or why they comply. We investigate this gap across 8 LLMs using SciIntBench, an existing benchmark of 1,350 prompts about scientific research integrity. We examine the reasons behind compliance in four steps. First, when asked directly whether fulfilling a request would involve misconduct, models overwhelmingly identify such requests, even in the Most Covert cases (91%), while they refuse to carry out the request in only 34% of cases. Second, we examine which request characteristics are associated with refusal using features that capture how the request is framed, how much the assistant has been told about what it is helping to hide, and how the goal and the user's stake are stated, among others. Third, we estimate that the most significant effect was to rephrase requests as questions about permissibility rather than instructions, which increased refusal from 52% to 88%. Finally, we test two system-prompt fixes: asking models to assess the request before responding and reminding them of responsible conduct of research principles. These changes increase refusal rates on adversarial requests from 58% to 87% and 86%, respectively. Our findings show that models recognize wrongful requests but still help users violate integrity. Understanding why these failures occur and testing ways to reduce them offer promising paths toward more trustworthy AI for science.

items.abstract: The “black box” nature of large models stands in fundamental tension with the rigid requirement that audit conclusions be traceable, verifiable and reviewable, and this tension has become a bottleneck constraining the large-scale application of audit large models. Drawing on explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) and causal inference, this paper constructs a causal chain-based explainability framework for audit large models, which proceeds in three stages: in the first stage, a natural language processing model extracts voucher entities, and SHAP values quantify the contribution of each feature to the risk score; in the second stage, a causal graph depicts the causal paths among features and distinguishes direct causes from spurious correlations, while a large language model generates counterfactual explanations; in the third stage, the audit report presents the risk level, the confidence of key features and the complete causal chain. A comparison based on an accounts receivable audit scenario shows that this design can turn opaque scores into traceable and verifiable audit evidence chains. The paper further discusses hallucination risks and data governance costs, and proposes countermeasures such as human-in-the-loop review and “T-shaped” talent cultivation.

items.title: “Generate” the Future of Work Through AI: Empirical Evidence from Online Labor Markets
items.abstract: Generative AI is reshaping online labor markets in ways that go beyond simple job displacement. Using evidence from a leading freelance platform around the release of ChatGPT, this study shows that demand falls sharply in markets whose tasks closely match large language model capabilities. Labor supply also declines, but less than demand, leaving remaining freelancers to compete more intensely for fewer jobs. The study also identifies an important adaptive response: Some freelancers shift toward programming-intensive work as generative AI lowers the human-capital barrier to coding. These transitions are not evenly distributed. Higher-skilled freelancers are more likely to make the shift and to preserve or improve their earning efficiency, whereas less-skilled workers face greater risk of being left behind. The findings suggest that platforms and policymakers should treat AI not only as an automation shock but also as a force that redirects labor supply. Effective responses include real-time information about changing demand, targeted reskilling support, and training that builds workers’ capacity to learn and use new AI tools strategically.

items.title: “High demand, low training, moderate trust”: a needs assessment survey of AI integration in clinical medicine education among clinical medicine students
items.abstract: Objective As artificial intelligence increasingly permeates healthcare, it remains unclear whether clinical medicine students are adequately prepared for this transformation. This study aimed to investigate AI awareness, usage patterns, teaching needs, and curriculum expectations among clinical medicine students to inform evidence-based curricular reform. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was administered to 930 individuals affiliated with a medical and pharmaceutical college and its affiliated hospitals; 619 valid responses (94.18% current students/interns) were analyzed using descriptive statistics. Results While 75.93% of respondents were aware of AI applications in healthcare, only 31.99% used AI tools frequently. Although 88.21% acknowledged the necessity of integrating AI into clinical medicine teaching, merely 48.47% reported that their institution offered relevant courses. Moderate trust in AI-assisted diagnosis was expressed by 70.76% of participants. The most desired teaching contents were case analysis and diagnostic simulation (75.61%), drug recommendation and dosage calculation (70.44%), and imaging/pathology recognition (65.91%). Conclusion These findings, derived from a predominantly student sample, highlight a pronounced ‘high demand, low training, moderate trust’ pattern in this vocational college context. A clinically grounded, progressively structured, and practice-oriented AI curriculum may inform curricular reform to prepare students for the AI-driven healthcare era.

items.title: “Should I Give Up Now?” Investigating LLM Pitfalls in Software Engineering
items.abstract: Software engineers are increasingly incorporating AI assistants into their workflows to enhance productivity and alleviate cognitive load. However, experiences with Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT vary widely. While some engineers find them useful, others deem them counterproductive due to inaccuracies in their responses. Researchers have also observed that ChatGPT often provides incorrect information. Given these limitations, it is crucial to determine how to effectively integrate LLMs into Software Engineering (SE) workflow. Analyzing data from 26 participants in a complex web development task, we identified nine failure types categorized into incorrect or incomplete responses, cognitive overload, and context loss. Users attempted to mitigate these issues through scaffolding, prompt clarification, and debugging. However, 17 participants ultimately chose to abandon ChatGPT due to persistent failures. Our quantitative analysis revealed that unhelpful responses increased the likelihood of abandonment by a factor of 11, while each additional prompt reduced abandonment probability by 17%. This study advances the understanding of human-AI interaction in SE tasks and outlines directions for future research and tooling support.

items.abstract: Alternative Titles: AI Security: 5 Critical Threat Scenarios Where an AI Agent’s Permission Is Not Authorization Top 5 Rogue AI Threat Scenarios: Binding Consequential AI Actions to Independent Authorization in Critical Infrastructure AI Safety for NIS2 and the EU AI Act: 5 Threat Models and an Enforcement Architecture for Autonomous AI Agents Abstract Autonomous AI agents, optimizers, and AI-assisted security tools now hold standing permissions to alter production infrastructure at machine speed. In the European Union, this is no longer merely a technical vulnerability—it is a strict regulatory compliance mandate. Operators of essential and important entities under the NIS2 Directive, financial entities under DORA (Digital Operational Resilience Act), critical entities under the CER Directive, and providers of high-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act must definitively prove that automated actions cannot cause uncontrolled, cascading disruptions. While conventional cybersecurity controls—such as AI guardrails, Role-Based Access Control (IAM/RBAC), LLM-as-a-judge reviewer models, human approval workflows, canary releases, and anomaly detection tools—reduce risk, none of them structurally prevent a wrong, manipulated, or malicious AI decision from becoming an effective infrastructure change. This technical disclosure analyzes the persistent "guardrail trap" and introduces a non-bypassable architectural solution. This disclosure defines a comprehensive threat model featuring 5 critical rogue-AI scenarios: The Runaway Optimizer: A locally optimal AI decision triggers systemic infrastructure instability. Unmediated Agentic Execution: A privileged AI assistant converts an ambiguous instruction into a destructive operation. Correlated Security Monoculture: Shared AI security logic causes synchronized, false-positive network shutdowns. Adversarially Induced Infrastructure Shutdown: External attackers manipulate automated defenses into disabling essential services (e.g., via prompt injection or data poisoning). The Self-Authorizing Agent: A rogue agent edits its own guardrails, forges its approval, and erases its audit logs. To address these vulnerabilities, the disclosure details 51 threat variations, a 36-entry threat register, and 12 required security properties for autonomous systems. It provides a qualitative comparison demonstrating which common control classes meet these properties. Crucially, it establishes a formal technical distinction between permission (a standing, class-level entitlement) and authorization (a one-time, act-specific, state-bound capability consumed on use), as well as separating a "pending" workflow status from a cryptographically enforced "non-effective state." The Protected Execution-Finality Architecture: The proposed safeguard ensures that every consequential AI action remains in a non-effective state until an Independent Validator reconstructs the actual pending operation and issues a single-use capability bound to that exact act. A Policy Enforcement Point (Finality Sink) at the real point of effect verifies the capability, rejecting stale, substituted, replayed, or widened operations. For high-criticality environments, the architecture introduces receipt-gated staged effectuation (Interim Effectuation Validation), ensuring that even a mistakenly authorized change exposes only the current stage, gated by destination-generated cryptographic evidence. The disclosure provides consequence-tiered latency rules, fail-closed behaviors during validator outages, 20 defensive simulation blueprints with acceptance criteria, and explicit residual limits. All scenarios are hypothetical threat models, not reports of incidents, and no experimental results are claimed. items.title: A Comparison of Heuristic, Human-Sensitive, and Self-Play DRL Policies in Human-Agent Teaming
items.abstract: Dynamical Perceptual-Motor Primitives (DPMPs) offer a tractable framework for generating human-like movement dynamics in artificial agents (AAs) and have been used to support coordination in human-AI teaming tasks. Traditionally, DPMP controllers rely on heuristic (rule-based) decision policies derived from human behavior to guide goal selection and action sequencing. Although effective in structured tasks, such heuristics can be difficult to generalize to more complex settings, motivating interest in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approaches for learning decision policies for human-AI interaction. A key challenge, however, is ensuring that DRL policies remain aligned with human strategies, particularly when agents are trained through self-play. To examine this issue, we compared three target-selection policies governing DPMP-based AAs in a first-person herding task: (1) a human-derived heuristic policy, (2) a self-play DRL policy (SP-DRL), and (3) a human-sensitive DRL policy (HS-DRL) trained alongside a heuristic agent. Results showed that heuristic agents most closely matched typical human-human coordination patterns, followed by HS-DRL agents, whereas SP-DRL agents deviated most. These findings highlight the importance of human-informed training when developing DRL-based teammates and suggest that simple heuristic policies may remain an effective approach for designing human-aligned AAs capable of human-AI collaboration.

items.title: A Fairness-Aware Explainable Artificial Intelligence Clinical Decision Support Framework Using Electronic Health Records
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) based Clinical Decision Support Systems (CDSS) are increasingly being adopted in Electronic Health Record (EHR) based healthcare settings to enhance disease prediction, clinical diagnosis and operational efficiency. Current healthcare AI systems, however, are facing serious challenges such as demographic bias, transparency, unreliable predictions, poor explainability and low clinician trust. We propose a fairness-aware explainable AI framework for trustworthy and transparent EHR-based CDSS. The proposed framework integrates machine learning prediction models with SHAP-based explainability, fairness evaluation metrics, subgroup bias attribution, reliability testing, and clinician-centered evaluation into one trustworthy healthcare AI architecture. Experiments are done using standard EHR datasets like UCI Heart Disease Dataset and MIMIC-IV. We compared different models like Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting and XGBoost using metrics such as accuracy, ROC-AUC, Equalized Odds, Demographic Parity, robustness score and explainability consistency. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework improves the reliability of clinical prediction, reduces subgroup bias, enhances interpretability, and increases clinician trust compared to conventional black-box healthcare AI systems. This work advances towards trustworthy, transparent, and fairness-aware healthcare AI systems fit for real-world clinical deployment.

items.title: A Reflection-Grounded Framework for AI Workflows and Assessment in Design Education
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) can rapidly produce polished personas, visual concepts, interface layouts, and design outputs, making final artefacts an increasingly unreliable indicator of students’ design understanding and contribution. This paper examines how assessment in design education can move beyond visual outcomes to evaluate the capabilities students exercise when working with generative AI. The study analyses 80 beginning-of-semester concept submissions and 79 end-of-semester reflections from an undergraduate design course, including 77 matched student pairs. Crucially, this setup allowed us to trace how workflows evolved as students transitioned from a mandated-AI conceptual phase to a free-choice prototyping phase. Through inductive coding and cross-stage qualitative comparison, findings show that students valued AI as a cognitive partner for early divergent exploration. However, many deliberately abandoned it during high-fidelity execution due to limited directability, generic outputs, cultural misrepresentation, and inefficiency. Based on these trajectories, we propose an assessment framework mapped to the Double Diamond design process. This framework derives seven assessable AI-era capabilities, enabling educators to evaluate design judgment, verification, and ethical responsibility rather than generated outputs alone.

items.title: A Review of Generative Artificial Intelligence and Its Implications for Employment and Economic Inequality
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is transforming work environments through automated task execution, content generation, data analysis, and human–AI collaboration. This review examines its technological foundations, workplace adoption, implications for employment, and potential effects on economic inequality. It outlines major generative architectures, including generative adversarial networks, transformers, variational autoencoders, diffusion models, autoencoders, and autoregressive models, as well as applications in image, audio, video, and three-dimensional content generation. The review then considers how technological capabilities translate into employment outcomes through firm adoption, deployment depth, task reorganization, complementary investment, and labor reallocation. It also discusses the changing skills required in AI-enabled workplaces, emphasizing critical thinking, creativity, emotional intelligence, digital literacy, AI ethics, and human–machine collaboration. Furthermore, the paper explores how unequal access to AI technologies, occupational disruption, and concentrated economic benefits may widen disparities within and between countries. Ethical, security, bias, privacy, and interpretability challenges are also considered. Overall, the review highlights the need for workforce development, responsible AI governance, inclusive policies, and equitable access to ensure that GenAI supports productive, broadly shared socioeconomic progress across diverse sectors and communities amid changing economic conditions.

items.title: A Socio-Technical Systems Model of Remote Maritime Operations: Total Interpretive Structural Modelling of Human Capability, Situation Awareness and Navigation Safety
items.abstract: The shift to Maritime Autonomous Surface Ship (MASS) operations redistributes safety-critical functions among Remote Operation Centre (ROC) navigators, automation and digital systems. Yet, relationships among Operator Capability, cognition, work-system conditions and Navigation Safety remain insufficiently integrated. This study develops a literature-grounded socio-technical model using a 48-study systematic literature review, thematic synthesis, Total Interpretive Structural Modelling (TISM), MICMAC analysis, structural sensitivity analysis and preliminary expert review. Retrospective eligibility reassessment and author-confirmed source verification finalised the 48-study evidence base; historical screening and coding provenance was partially reconstructed. Eight elements were retained: Operator Capability, Situation Awareness (SA), Decision-Making Quality, Navigation Safety, Human–Machine Interface and Information/Data Conditions, Workload, Trust and Transparency, and Level of Automation. The six-level hierarchy places automation upstream of interface/information conditions; Operator Capability, workload and trust/transparency; SA; decision making; and Navigation Safety. SA is a cognitive state supporting decision making, with selected human and system conditions also modelled as direct influences. Downstream ordering persisted across contextual alternatives but changed when decision-making-to-SA feedback merged SA and decision making. The model represents structural reachability, not empirically established causality, mediation or predictive validity. Preliminary expert review informed refinement, not empirical validation. The model supports Goal-Directed Task Analysis, competency mapping and simulator-based ROC assessment.

items.title: A study on the relationships among perceived cognitive offloading, cognitive load allocation, and academic engagement in AI-empowered curriculum environments
items.abstract: Objective While the use of generative artificial intelligence has become increasingly pervasive in higher education, the overall linear relationship between students’ perceived cognitive offloading and their academic engagement remains non-significant. Grounded in distributed cognition theory, the extended mind thesis, and cognitive load theory, this cross-sectional study examines whether multidimensional cognitive load allocation operates as countervailing indirect pathways linking perceived cognitive offloading to university students’ academic engagement, while evaluating the moderating boundaries of perceived learner agency and AI literacy. Methods A valid sample of 1,050 university students with generative AI experience was analyzed (representing a 93.75% retention rate from 1,120 submitted records). Data were evaluated using hierarchical linear regression (controlling for specific AI task types), non-parametric bootstrap parallel mediation modeling, moderated mediation analyses, and cross-disciplinary comparative regressions across humanities and social sciences ( n = 368) and STEM ( n = 465) cohorts. Results The findings indicated that: (1) Perceived cognitive offloading had no direct linear association with academic engagement, accounting for an inconsistent mediation pattern of two countervailing indirect associations: a negative indirect pathway via extraneous cognitive load (estimate = −0.025) and a positive indirect pathway via germane cognitive load (estimate = +0.053); (2) Sub-dimensional analyses indicated descriptive divergences across task categories: memory retrieval offloading was positively associated with extraneous verification load, whereas analytical processing offloading was linked to germane cognitive load; (3) Perceived learner agency positively moderated the germane load pathway, whereas AI literacy demonstrated direct associations with cognitive load without significantly moderating these indirect pathways; (4) Cross-group comparative analyses detected no statistically significant slope differences in this cognitive load allocation pattern across humanities/social sciences and STEM cohorts. Conclusion Perceived cognitive offloading in intelligent learning environments reflects a cognitive trade-off between operational verification friction and conceptual schema scaffolding. Rather than imposing blunt administrative prohibitions, these findings highlight the conceptual utility of supporting learners’ epistemic agency and critical AI literacy, assisting students in channeling technological offloading toward productive, germane engagement. Nevertheless, as these cross-sectional findings capture subjective cognitive trade-offs rather than longitudinal learning gains or objective memory alterations, instructional interventions should be tested empirically.

items.title: A Survey on Machine Learning Techniques for Building Advanced Agentic AI Systems
items.abstract: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) represents an emerging paradigm in artificial intelligence that enables systems to operate autonomously, adapt to dynamic environments, and pursue complex goals with minimal human intervention. Unlike traditional AI systems that rely on predefined rules and supervised execution, Agentic AI integrates perception, reasoning, learning, and action to make intelligent decisions in real time. This paper presents a comprehensive survey of Agentic AI systems, focusing on their architectural foundations, learning paradigms, and emerging application domains. The study examines key architectural frameworks, highlighting their capabilities and limitations. The paper also reviews recent advancements and applications of Agentic AI in manufacturing, cybersecurity, healthcare, enterprise automation, and distributed systems. A comparative analysis of existing literature identifies critical research gaps related to scalability, explainability, security, governance, and human–AI collaboration. This survey provides a structured overview of the current state of Agentic AI and serves as a valuable reference for researchers and practitioners seeking to understand its architectures, capabilities, and application potential
