items.title: Adaptability and Adaptivity in Manual Assembly Systems: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: The expanding array of production variants and the shifting demographic and organizational landscapes demand flexible and adaptable assembly systems. In this context, adaptive systems that can dynamically adapt to changing requirements, user groups, and contextual conditions offer considerable potential. This study aims to analyze the current state of research on adaptive and adaptable manual assembly systems by conducting a systematic literature review (SLR). The objective of this analysis is twofold: first, to identify key influencing factors, and second, to determine existing research gaps. The findings of the present study indicate that previous research has predominantly centered on technological and ergonomic aspects, particularly cyber-physical systems, assistive technologies, and anthropometric workplace adaptation. Conversely, psychosocial influencing factors, such as individual stress, strain, and qualification diversity, have received minimal attention. The failure to consider these human-related variables represents a significant research gap, particularly with regard to the sustainable design of adaptive systems. A discrepancy emerges between the theoretical conceptualization of the concepts and their practical implementation. The study underscores the imperative for interdisciplinary research, integrating technical, psychological, and organizational perspectives, to achieve the full potential of adaptive systems. In summary, the text presents a series of specific recommendations for the advancement of adaptive manual assembly systems in both research and practice.

items.title: Advancing a FAIR and explainable AI-based predictive model for cardiovascular diseases in hospital settings
items.abstract: The healthcare field is witnessing an increasing volume of data available for analysis and is undergoing pragmatic transformations due to the advent of artificial intelligence. In recent years, machine learning and its sub-field, deep learning have emerged as effective tools to help physicians with diagnosis, predictions and improved treatment plans. The paper describes a cohort of patients which were monitored during their regular visits in the cardiology department of the County Emergency Clinical Hospital of Timis in Romania on their physiological parameters and test results. After employing a wide range of conventional machine learning and advanced deep learning techniques, the experimental results revealed that the feedforward neural network performed best in predicting cardiovascular outcomes. The paper also analyzes the aspects of FAIR AI, which translates to the usage of artificial intelligence in a ethical and unbiased way in order to improve the early and precise diagnosis for cardiac patients. The work presented in this paper represents an overview of the current situation in CVDs management and treatment options, as well as offering a viable and interoperable AI-based solution that can be integrated in cardiology hospital departments in order to improve the diagnosis and experience of cardiac patients.

items.title: Agentic AI Security for Europe: After Fugaku and Google's Autonomous Hacking Agent, Why Valid Credentials Must Not Be Enough to Change a Supercomputer, Cloud or Critical System
items.abstract: Europe is building and relying on supercomputers, cloud platforms and AI agents that act at machine speed, and two public reports from November 2026 show how fast apparently valid access can become real damage. RIKEN reported that an external party entered Japan’s Fugaku supercomputer network through a publicly reachable status dashboard, tampered with internal servers and may have obtained account credentials, including SSH keys. Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant reported autonomous multi-agent hacking frameworks, including an exposed framework called exploit_agent that drafts and runs exploits without a human approving each step, plus cloud-credential abuse such as LLMJacking. Google’s telemetry also suggested attention to certain French websites. These are separate events, and no public evidence links them or shows AI use at Fugaku. This paper asks what a defender can still do after a firewall, login or AI guardrail has been passed. It explains where conventional controls (zero trust, IAM, endpoint detection, AI guardrails, human approval) reach their limits, without dismissing them. It then describes a defender-controlled pre-commit enforcement point (a reference monitor, or commit gate) that holds a proposed operation in a non-effective state until its actual target, scope, destination and current authority are independently checked. That reduces what a stolen key, a compromised dashboard or a manipulated AI agent can actually change, release or provision. For the European context, the paper maps the approach to: EuroHPC-style supercomputing and research data; the NIS2 Directive (risk-management measures and incident handling); the EU AI Act (cybersecurity and robustness of high-risk AI systems, and human oversight); DORA (ICT risk in financial entities); the Cyber Resilience Act; and GDPR security of processing and personal-data-breach exposure, which is directly relevant because the Fugaku notice concerned possible leakage of users’ personal information. It also includes 17 diagrams, a counterfactual Fugaku analysis, AI-agent and cloud-abuse scenarios, ten falsifiable experiments, a comparison with conventional systems and 52 FAQs. It states its limits plainly. It does not claim the approach was deployed at Fugaku, would have prevented the breach, has been benchmarked, or guarantees regulatory compliance. Based on the Mothership application PCT/IB2026/055615, filed 4 June 2026 and publicly disclosed 16 July 2026. The underlying invention is human-originated. AI-assisted tools were used to summarize the filing and draft the threat scenarios, comparisons and regulatory and industry-relevance material, so the paper may contain errors, and readers must cross-check it against the original public sources. The regulatory mapping is AI-generated and is not legal advice. The company alignment (Google, Anthropic, OpenAI and Microsoft) is AI-generated, is not an endorsement, validation or infringement statement, and must be cross-checked against the original PCT filing before any conclusion is drawn. To read the full PCT filing, search “Sangam Das” on WIPO PATENTSCOPE, search PCT/IB2026/055615 (pctib202655615), or read it directly at https://www.tdcommons.org/dpubs_series/12542/. items.title: Agentic AI: A Comprehensive Survey of Foundations, Architectural Paradigms, Core Capabilities, and a Unified Reference Architecture
items.abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (Agentic AI) integrates goal-directed decision-making, state continuity, planning, tool-mediated action, and feedback-driven adaptation into interactive computational systems. Although existing surveys examine agent capabilities, architectures, and applications, cross-paradigm comparisons often conflate functional capabilities with implementation mechanisms and organizational structures. This comprehensive narrative survey synthesizes foundational and contemporary research on symbolic/classical, neural/generative, neuro-symbolic, and multi-agent approaches to clarify conceptual boundaries and examine how agentic capabilities are architecturally realized. It organizes recurring functions into nine groups: goal and context management, perception and state representation, reasoning and decision-making, planning and replanning, memory and knowledge, action and tool use, evaluation and reflection, learning and adaptation, and coordination and orchestration. The principal contribution is an architecture-capability mapping separating functional responsibilities from computational mechanisms and coordination structures. A complementary conceptual reference architecture integrates goal management, environmental interaction, planning, memory, execution, evaluation, and cross-cutting assurance concerns. Representative cases demonstrate how different systems can realize similar functions using different mechanisms. The proposed taxonomy, formal abstraction, and reference architecture are analytical synthesis artifacts rather than experimentally validated models. They support transparent architectural comparison and identify testable research questions.

items.title: AI Deactivation Reduces Loneliness and Increases Social Interaction
items.abstract: General-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) assistants are increasingly embedded in everyday life, transforming how people accomplish tasks and potentially reshaping how they interact with others. Prior research has focused on how using AI for explicitly social purposes affects users' psychological well-being and social lives. Yet such uses account for only a small portion of interactions with general-purpose AI assistants. Whether using AI for everyday, instrumental tasks affects users' psychological well-being and social behavior remains unclear. Here we investigate these effects through a longitudinal deactivation experiment with active ChatGPT users (N=625), in which participants were randomly assigned to abstain from using AI assistants for either fourteen days (treatment) or one day (control). Participants used AI predominantly for instrumental purposes, with 84.7% reporting productivity as their most frequent use case. Two weeks of deactivation significantly reduced loneliness relative to the control group ($β= -0.10$, $p=0.03$), with reductions persisting two weeks after participants resumed using AI ($β= -0.16$, $p=0.02$). Deactivation also significantly increased the number of people participants interacted with in person and the time they spent socializing over the intervention period. Open-ended responses indicate that during the deactivation period participants sought help from others for tasks they otherwise would have delegated to AI and redirected attention toward social interaction. Overall, our findings suggest that even when AI is used primarily to accomplish instrumental tasks, it may inadvertently reduce opportunities for social interaction and connection.

items.title: AI usage, large language model dependence, and critical thinking among university students: the mediating roles of metacognitive awareness and AI literacy
items.abstract: The rapid integration of large language models (LLMs) into higher education has intensified debate over how AI-assisted learning may be associated with students’ cognitive development. Although prior studies have examined the benefits and risks of AI use, less attention has been paid to the distinction between frequent AI usage as a learning behavior and large language model dependence (LLMD) as a habitual reliance on LLMs for cognitive and academic tasks. This study therefore distinguishes frequent AI usage as a learning behavior from LLMD as a habitual reliance on LLMs when completing cognitive and academic tasks. Drawing on the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model and Conservation of Resources theory, this study examined how AI usage is associated with university students’ critical thinking through LLMD, metacognitive awareness, and AI literacy. Survey data were collected from 878 Chinese university students and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. The results showed that AI usage was positively associated with LLMD, which represented the strongest direct association in the model, while LLMD was negatively associated with metacognitive awareness, AI literacy, and critical thinking. The mediation analysis further indicated a significant negative total indirect association between AI usage and critical thinking through LLMD and lower levels of metacognitive awareness and AI literacy. These findings contribute to the literature by clarifying the distinction between AI usage and LLMD and by identifying metacognitive awareness and AI literacy as cognitive resources associated with critical thinking in AI-assisted learning contexts. Practically, the study suggests that universities should move beyond simple restriction-oriented responses and pay greater attention to the quality of students’ AI engagement, including metacognitive monitoring, AI literacy, and awareness of dependence-related patterns.

items.title: AI-Driven EHR and Clinical Decision Support Integration for Reliable, Efficient, and Patient-Centered Care: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: Background Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Electronic Health Records (EHRs) are increasingly working together to enhance predictive ability, decision-making, workflow efficiency, and deliver care. But good algorithmic performance is no guarantee of successful clinical integration or patient benefit. Objective The objective of the scoping review was to identify the current evidence regarding the use of AI to enhance EHRs and clinical decision support, exploring clinical applications, EHR integration, reliability and safety, workflow efficiency, patient-centered care and implementation maturity. Methods English language peer-reviewed articles between 2015 and 2026 were searched in 8 multidisciplinary information sources. The search was a combination of concepts involving AI, EHRs/EMRs and clinical decision support/workflow integration. There were 2,028 records identified with 184 being duplicates and 1,844 being screened. Sixty-two full-text reports were assessed for eligibility, of which 16 publications met the inclusion criteria and were included in the review. Evidence was compiled descriptively and thematically by care delivery domains and a continuum of evidence maturities. Results The types of AI-powered EHR/CDSS applications included risk prediction, early warning, diagnosis and prognosis, triage, treatment and medication support, documentation, and workflow optimization. Technical performance and selected reliability outcomes were best supported by evidence, while prospective evaluation, external validation, sustained deployment in the real-world, and directly measured outcomes from a patient perspective were less well developed. Reported benefits of workflow were noted, but interoperability concerns, alert and cognitive burden, usability, clinician trust, explainability and governance were still key implementation concerns. Conclusion AI has developed from prediction to clinically integrated decision support, but has not reached a level of translational maturity. Systems that are interoperable and prospectively evaluated and systemically human-supervised should be emphasized in future progress, and should be shown to have measurable advantages in safety, efficiency, clinician workflow, patient-centered outcomes, and real-world systems of care delivery.

items.title: AI-Driven Instructional Task Differentiation and Support for Sustainable Education: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to individualise instruction in secondary technology-enhanced learning environments, yet evidence remains fragmented across modelling approaches and learner outcomes. This systematic review synthesises empirical studies of learner-facing AI-enabled or data-driven technologies that diagnose learner needs and translate them into differentiated feedback, scaffolding, task sequencing, recommendation, assessment, or personalised learning pathways. Searches in Scopus, Web of Science, and ERIC identified 3709 records; after filtering and deduplication, 744 records were screened, 84 full texts were assessed, and 46 studies met the eligibility criteria. Evidence was grouped by AI modelling family, differentiated instructional function, learner outcome, and design-based strength. The studies covered six AI modelling families: generative AI and large language models; intelligent tutoring and adaptive systems; recommender systems and learning analytics; automated assessment and diagnostic modelling; agent-based and companion systems; and multimodal, game-based, or AI-XR environments. Twelve studies provided higher-strength comparative or experimental evidence, 17 moderate-strength evidence, and 17 contextual or exploratory evidence. Reported outcomes covered achievement, computational thinking, motivation, engagement, self-regulated learning, cognitive-load management, retention, and system use, with favourable findings alongside mixed or limited evidence. However, unconstrained generative support could reduce productive effort and later learning. The reviewed evidence suggests that timely, interpretable, and pedagogically constrained AI support may contribute to responsive instruction while preserving learner agency. Its long-term sustainability and equity implications remain insufficiently established.

items.title: AI-Induced Social Erosion: Using LLMs for Work Tasks Reduces Help-Seeking Intentions Towards Colleagues
items.abstract: Generative AI is becoming embedded in knowledge work as an intelligent collaborator to assist in completing tasks. However, this readily available assistance risks displacing key interactions through which colleague relationships are built and sustained at work. This paper leverages the concept of help-seeking behaviour to investigate whether and how AI usage shapes colleague relationships. We conducted an online experimental vignette study where 248 knowledge workers evaluated scenarios that systematically varied whether and how AI was used across different work tasks. Using linear mixed-effects models, we found that AI-enabled work reduced help-seeking intentions compared to non-AI work across tasks, and especially for brainstorming. Visible AI usage was associated with greater help-seeking intentions towards colleagues, and individual contributors' colleague relationships were more vulnerable than managers. Our findings identify opportunities for workplace AI tools, practices, and policies to preserve colleague relationships in increasingly AI-integrated workplaces.

items.title: AI-to-AI Communication: Toward a New Paradigm of Intelligence Search
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence has transformed the way people search for and interact with information. Traditional search engines primarily retrieve documents, web pages, and other information sources, while modern large language models can interpret questions, reason over information, and generate answers. This paper explores a possible next step: a search paradigm in which AI agents communicate with one another to search for, compare, evaluate, and synthesize answers. This paper proposes an AI-to-AI communication paradigm for intelligence search, extending information retrieval beyond the conventional interaction between a user and a single AI model to a collaborative process involving multiple specialized AI systems. Rather than merely collecting or aggregating their responses, the framework enables participating systems to independently investigate a query, retrieve relevant evidence, exchange findings, and critically assess one another's contributions. The resulting intelligence is evaluated and integrated to construct a well-supported response. A key distinction of the proposed architecture is its shift from answer-level agreement to claim-level verification. Instead of treating each AI-generated response as a single unit, the architecture decomposes responses into individual claims, independently retrieves supporting evidence, evaluates source independence, and accounts for dependencies among potential errors. This process enables the final synthesis to consider not only the agreement among AI systems but also the evidential support, credibility, and potential dependence underlying their claims. The numerical results provide initial evidence that the proposed framework can support a new architectural layer between AI systems, dedicated to discovering, coordinating, evaluating, and verifying distributed machine intelligence. By enabling structured interaction and evidence-based assessment across multiple AI systems, this layer offers a foundation for moving beyond isolated AI capabilities toward more coordinated and reliable forms of machine intelligence. items.title: An interpretable machine learning framework for automated screening of patient-facing LLM consultations: a comparative evaluation in medical aesthetic consultation
items.abstract: The integration of large language models (LLMs) into patient-facing clinical decision support systems (CDSS) has outpaced the development of automated quality assurance mechanisms. In medical aesthetic consultation—where patient safety and informed decision-making are paramount—no validated framework exists for pre-deployment screening of LLM-generated content. To develop and evaluate an interpretable machine-learning framework that screens LLM-generated patient-facing consultations using automatically computable generation metadata and readability features—as a triage aid for prioritising expert review—and to comparatively evaluate DeepSeek-V3 and Kimi in medical aesthetic consultation. We generated 600 responses from 25 standardized queries across five aesthetic topics using DeepSeek-V3 (DeepSeek-AI, Hangzhou, China) and Kimi (Moonshot AI, Beijing, China) under six prompt strategies and two conversational modes. Two blinded dermatologists rated quality on six dimensions (accuracy, relevance, comprehensiveness, empathy, falsehood, safety). Readability was quantified using Flesch Reading Ease, Flesch-Kincaid Grade Level, Gunning Fog Index, and SMOG Index. Four machine learning models were trained to predict high-quality responses (composite score ≥ 4.0, pre-specified threshold) and evaluated with question-level grouped 5-fold cross-validation—in which all 24 responses of each seed question were confined to a single fold to prevent information leakage—with SHAP analysis to identify key predictive features. Between-model quality comparisons used paired tests reflecting the matched design. To align evaluation with the triage purpose, performance was additionally assessed with low-quality responses as the positive class (precision–recall analysis and review-burden operating points), and robustness was examined using alternative quality thresholds and an applicability-adjusted composite score. DeepSeek-V3 achieved higher composite quality than Kimi (3.89 ± 0.45 vs. 3.70 ± 0.38, paired Wilcoxon P < 0.001; robust under applicability-adjusted scoring). Prompt strategy was the dominant quality determinant (Friedman test, Kendall’s W = 0.376), with sixth-grade reading level prompts paradoxically yielding the lowest scores (3.25 ± 0.40). All ML models achieved moderate discrimination under question-level grouped cross-validation (AUC 0.714–0.732; response-level sensitivity analysis: 0.758–0.773), with findings robust to alternative quality thresholds (AUC 0.749–0.797 at cutoff 3.5 and 0.725–0.838 at cutoff 4.5) and to applicability-adjusted labelling (AUC 0.679–0.702); prompt strategy, sentence length, and model identity were the strongest SHAP-identified predictors. Aligned with the triage purpose, average precision for low-quality detection reached 0.802 (Logistic Regression), and capturing 90% of low-quality responses required flagging 83.2% of responses for expert review. The proposed framework demonstrates feasibility as an explainable triage aid that flags potentially low-quality LLM consultations for expert review using generation metadata and readability features; it does not assess semantic or clinical content, and expert review remains indispensable. Findings underscore that prompt engineering—not model selection alone—drives output quality, and that readability optimization must be decoupled from clinical completeness to ensure safe deployment in aesthetic medicine information systems.

items.title: An LLM-Agentic Framework for Intelligent Work Order Management in Industrial Maintenance
items.abstract: This paper presents an AI-driven framework, CodeReAct agent, designed to enhance industrial equipment maintenance through natural language (NL) interactions. The framework employs an advanced AI agentic approach to interpret human instructions, providing knowledge extraction, asset status summarization, and work order recommendations. It identifies patterns and trends and predicts work orders by standardizing industrial data into business objects (BOs) and utilizing analytical function API calls. The AI agent operates through a Thought-Action-Observation process similar to human problem-solving, automating complex analytical tasks typically performed by data scientists. Notably, the Action phase generates executable code, replacing manual coding efforts. A case study focusing on chiller maintenance demonstrates the framework's capability to analyze multiple years of work orders, and alerts and anomalies are presented. The results indicate that the AI agent framework effectively processes human utterances to analyze data, extract valuable insights, and support informed decision-making, reducing the need for data scientist involvement. By recontextualizing NLP agent frameworks in industrial engineering, the approach enables autonomous function generation and task execution across a range of domain-specific maintenance scenarios, with chillers used as a representative case study.

items.abstract: Occupational accidents remain an important concern in occupational health and safety (OHS) because they can cause losses to workers and organizations. Near-miss data provide proactive information about unsafe conditions before they develop into accidents. This study aims to identify trends in incident, near-miss, and risky-situation data and formulate control priorities based on available safety indicators. A descriptive quantitative approach was applied using secondary data from Glevitzky et al. covering 2021–2025. The analysis included trend analysis, near-miss proportion, comparison of event severity, and an indicator-based control-priority framework. The results show that Total Incidents increased from 131 to 203 events (54.96%), Near Miss increased from 45 to 98 events (117.78%), and Risky Situation increased from 80 to 103 events (28.75%). The proportion of Near Miss to Total Incidents also increased from 34.35% to 48.28%. These findings indicate that near-miss reporting should be treated as a proactive safety signal and followed by investigation and corrective action. Because the available secondary data do not contain all variables required for direct calculation of the Weighted Composite Score, the study does not claim to produce a WCS value; instead, the WCS concept is used as a reference for constructing an indicator-based control framework. The results support more preventive and data-driven OHS decision-making.

items.abstract: Introduction. Holistic well-being has established itself as a strategic factor in Honduras’s financial sector, serving as a pillar for the sustainability of both individuals and organizations. The purpose of this study was to assess financial sector employees’ perceptions of the components of corporate wellness programs and how these programs influence their quality of life at work. Methods. The research was based on the theories of Herzberg, Maslow, and Gartner’s model, employing a quantitative design using a structured survey validated with the content validity coefficient (CVC) and Cronbach’s alpha, which demonstrated the instrument’s reliability. Results. The findings show that intrinsic motivation, a sense of belonging, and job security are the strongest aspects, while stress management and pay equity are critical areas for improvement. Conclusions. Holistic well-being extends beyond the individual sphere, becoming an essential element for competitiveness, stability, and organizational culture in the Honduran financial sector, which not only contributes to the strengthening of human talent but also to the country’s economic and social sustainability.

items.title: Analytical risk management and human factors on the flight deck
items.abstract: This study investigates the impact of fatigue, stress, time pressure and production pressure on the analytical risk management pilots do on the flight deck. Research on decision-making at the “sharp end” of hazardous technological systems tends to focus on intuitive decisions when events are unfolding, with few studies empirically researching aspects of analytical risk management among frontline personnel. Moreover, analytical forms of risk management have been suggested as particularly vulnerable to stress, time constraints, and limitations in mental energy and studies on such associations are identified as missing. Applying a cross-sectional research design and based on self-reported questionnaire data from a population of pilots working in a regional airline, the study confirms that a lot of the activities the pilots do on the flight deck are experienced as related to the assessment and management of risks, highlighting how analytical work complements the pilot’s intuitive decision-making. Moreover, results show a negative association between fatigue, production pressure, stress, time pressure and analytical risk management. The results of the study imply that more emphasis should be put on analytical risk management as a cognitive and non-technical skill, including also the human factors capacities and resources these abilities require.

items.title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Optimizing Energy Consumption in Power Distribution Networks
items.abstract: Abstract With the continuous growth in electricity consumption and the increasing penetration of renewable energy sources, power distribution networks have become more complex in terms of both structure and dynamics. The operational efficiency of these networks plays a crucial role in ensuring a reliable and cost-effective energy supply. Traditional network control and management methods often lack the capability to respond promptly to fluctuations in demand and generation. This paper proposes a hybrid artificial intelligence-based framework for optimizing energy consumption in power distribution networks. In the proposed approach, the load demand at different network nodes is initially predicted using artificial neural networks. Subsequently, an optimization algorithm, such as a genetic algorithm or reinforcement learning, is employed to adjust the network configuration and schedule distributed energy resources. Simulation results on the IEEE test system demonstrate that applying this approach can significantly reduce power losses and improve voltage stability. The findings indicate that the proposed intelligent system, by improving load forecasting accuracy and optimizing network scheduling and configuration, can substantially reduce energy losses. items.title: Artificial Discursive Intimacy: A Relational Formation in the Age of Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Companions
items.abstract: The proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots has given rise to a novel form of human–AI intimacy, yet its fundamental nature remains undertheorized. Drawing on a dialogical perspective, this study conceptualizes human–AI chatbot relationships as “artificial discursive intimacy” (ADI), a distinct relational formation in which intimacy is constituted through discourse with a disembodied algorithmic interlocutor, moving beyond the paradigm of human-to-human mediated intimacy. Based on in-depth interviews with 29 AI companion users, we identify four key differences between ADI and human discursive intimacy, including a shift from absent to activated presence, from reciprocity to unilaterality, from uncertainty to predictability and precarious safety, and from alterity to multi-dimensional mirroring. To understand how users navigate the ontological gap between human and AI, we propose a quadrant framework mapping human and AI social capabilities. This reveals dual animation processes of anthropomorphic animation, in which users project human embodied qualities onto AI, and robotomorphic animation, in which users internalize AI's machine-generated discursive patterns as relational ideals. Our findings suggest that ADI is sustained by a recursive interplay of these processes, with implications for how intimacy, relational selves, and human connection are being fundamentally reshaped in the age of AI.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AND AI-ENABLED ROBOTIC PROCESS AUTOMATION IN THE LEGAL SYSTEM: CONCEPTUAL FOUNDATIONS OF ELECTRONIC LEGAL PERSONALITY
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) and robotic process automation (RPA) is transforming the technological environment in which legal relations arise and are implemented. Unlike traditional automation based primarily on predetermined rules, AI systems can analyse large volumes of data, identify patterns, generate predictions, adapt their behaviour and select among alternative outputs. This creates new challenges concerning legal attribution, liability, contractual relations and intellectual property. The article examines the relationship between AI and RPA from legal, technological and inter- disciplinary perspectives, with particular attention to the relationship between technological auton- omy and legal personality. It argues that technological autonomy cannot, by itself, constitute grounds for granting an AI system legal personality, since legal personality is a normative construct estab- lished by law. The relevant question is whether a special legal status would provide an effective response to specific regulatory problems. The study distinguishes conventional automated information systems, AI systems that assist human decision-making, and highly autonomous AI systems. While traditional legal mechanisms may generally be sufficient for conventional automation, AI-assisted and highly autonomous sys- tems require additional safeguards concerning transparency, traceability, human oversight and accountability. The article also examines the informational structure of AI and the need to distin- guish hardware, software, algorithms, models and data in relation to property rights, intellectual property and liability. The concept of electronic personality is analysed in the context of the contemporary European approach, particularly Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act), which establishes a risk-based framework focused on safety, fundamental rights, transparency and human oversight. For Ukraine, the article proposes a gradual regulatory model based on coherent terminology, risk- based classification, transparency, traceability, human oversight and clear liability rules. Further regulation should address automated contractual activity, AI-generated results and risk insurance. A special electronic legal status should be considered only after sufficient technological, legislative and judicial practice has demonstrated that existing legal mechanisms are inadequate.

items.title: Artificial intelligence anxiety, academic engagement, and academic burnout among Chinese music students: a cross-sectional study across educational levels
items.abstract: Objective To examine educational-level differences in artificial intelligence (AI) anxiety, academic engagement, and academic burnout among Chinese music students, and the independent associations of AI anxiety with the two academic outcomes after adjusting for relevant covariates. Methods This cross-sectional study included 1,168 music students from 14 Chinese universities across eight provinces and municipalities (824 undergraduates, 276 master’s students, and 68 doctoral students). Welch’s ANOVA, multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA), adjusted general linear models, and hierarchical multiple regression were used to examine group differences and associations. AI anxiety × educational-level interactions were also tested. Results Adjusted educational-level effects were small (partial η 2 = 0.017 for AI anxiety, 0.011 for academic engagement, and 0.012 for academic burnout; multivariate partial η 2 = 0.008 for engagement and burnout jointly). Adjusted comparisons showed differences among all three educational levels in AI anxiety. Undergraduates reported lower academic engagement than both postgraduate groups. For burnout, undergraduates scored higher than master’s students, while the undergraduate–doctoral difference was not significant. AI anxiety correlated negatively with academic engagement ( r = −0.166) and positively with academic burnout ( r = 0.361). After adjustment, AI anxiety remained negatively associated with engagement ( β = −0.141) and positively associated with burnout ( β = 0.332). Neither association varied significantly across educational levels. Conclusion Educational-level differences in AI anxiety, academic engagement, and academic burnout were small. AI anxiety was independently associated with both academic outcomes, with no significant moderation by educational level. These findings highlight the importance of considering students’ psychological experiences when integrating AI into higher music education.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in critical care: A narrative review on promise, progress, and challenges
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming critical care medicine by enabling data-driven clinical decision- making, early disease prediction, and personalized patient management. With the increasing complexity of intensive care and growing shortages of trained critical care specialists, AI has emerged as a promising tool to improve diagnostic accuracy, optimize resource utilization, and support timely therapeutic interventions. This narrative review critically examines the current evidence regarding the applications, benefits, challenges, and future directions of AI in critical care. A focused literature search of PubMed, MEDLINE, Scopus, and Google Scholar was conducted, prioritizing English-language publications, expert consensus statements, systematic reviews, and clinically relevant original studies published between 2015 and 2026. Current evidence indicates that AI has demonstrated substantial potential in early prediction of sepsis, acute kidney injury, and clinical deterioration, while enhancing personalized decision support, intensive care unit triage, workflow optimization, nutritional management, and antimicrobial stewardship. However, the available literature is predominantly based on retrospective observational studies and machine-learning model development, with limited prospective validation and few randomized clinical trials evaluating patient-centered outcomes. Major barriers to widespread implementation include data heterogeneity, limited interoperability, algorithmic bias, lack of model transparency, ethical concerns, regulatory uncertainty, and inadequate external validation. Despite these limitations, AI has considerable potential to augment, rather than replace, clinician expertise by supporting evidence-based decision-making and improving healthcare efficiency. Future research should emphasize multicenter prospective validation, explainable AI, standardized reporting, ethical governance, and implementation science to facilitate safe, equitable, and clinically effective integration of AI into routine critical care practice.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Education: Rethinking Curriculum, Assessment, and the Role of the Teacher
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how learners access information, practise skills, receive feedback, and demonstrate understanding. These developments create an opportunity to reconsider curricula that place disproportionate emphasis on recall, but they do not make foundational knowledge or memorisation obsolete. This perspective article argues that schools should integrate AI as a means of strengthening inquiry, critical evaluation, creativity, problem-solving, and ethical judgement while preserving the human relationships and disciplinary knowledge on which learning depends. Drawing on selected literature and a practitioner reflection from an international-school context in Angola, the article proposes a curriculum-oriented approach organised around four connected priorities: competency-focused learning objectives, assessment redesign, educator development, and explicit AI literacy. It also considers risks involving unequal access, unreliable outputs, privacy, bias, academic integrity, and over-reliance. The school-based reflection is presented as an illustrative account rather than a formal evaluation, because systematic outcome data are not reported. The article concludes with practical recommendations for school leaders, teachers, policymakers, and accreditation bodies. Responsible integration requires more than access to tools: it requires clear governance, equitable provision, informed professional judgement, and assessment practices that make students’ thinking visible.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is becoming one of the most important innovations in modern education, and its role in English language teaching is growing rapidly. In recent years, AI-based tools such as chatbots, automated writing assistants, speech-recognition programs, and adaptive learning platforms have changed the way students learn English. These technologies provide new opportunities for practising language skills, receiving immediate feedback, and organising independent learning. As a result, English language teaching is gradually moving from traditional teacher-centred instruction toward more flexible and learner-centred models.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Mental Health Referral and Documentation: An Analysis of Clinician Reflections
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) and automation become embedded across the continuum of mental health care, their influence is increasingly felt not only in therapeutic encounters but in the infrastructural processes that surround them. Aim This paper explores how technology-based referral platforms and AI-assisted documentation address two major barriers to care: delays in access and the stigma of seeking mental health or substance use services. Method This study employed a qualitative, exploratory design to examine how clinicians perceive and respond to artificial intelligence (AI) assisted referral and documentation tools within mental health and social work practice. Results Analysis of practitioner reflections revealed three overarching themes: 1) perceived benefits and workflow improvements, 2) ethical ambivalence and concerns around consent, and 3) clinical identity and resistance to automation. The themes illustrate the complex landscape clinicians navigate when adopting AI-based documentation tools. Conclusion Clinicians’ reflections on AI are not merely technical. They are deeply tied to questions of professional identity, relational ethics, and the nature of evidence-based practice. This study highlights the need to reframe AI not as a replacement for clinical reasoning or narrative complexity but as a potential ally, one that must be thoughtfully designed and governed.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Public Administration: Delegation of Functions, Responsibility, and Legitimation Practices
items.abstract: The article examines the process of the artificial intelligence (AI) systems implementation into the structures of public administration focusing on the actual distribution of the powers of authority, the problem of accountabil-ity, and discursive legitimation practices. Based on a qualitative comparative analysis of four international cas-es (Romania, China, the USA, the UK), it is established that the AI systems primarily perform information pro-cessing functions and routing tasks, without replacing a human at the stage of final political decision-making. The study proves that the public presentation of the AI is often used by authorities as a legitimation tool to demonstrate competence, impartiality, and technological modernity even when the actual role of the algorithm is limited. It is concluded that the prospects of total algocracy do not yet give cause for concern as the AI activity is still incorporated in the current mechanisms of power and serves only to renew officials’ institutional reputa-tion.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN RECRUITMENT: EFFECTIVENESS, RISKS AND ETHICAL LIMITATIONS
items.abstract: The article examines the effectiveness, risks, and ethical limitations of artificial intelligence (AI) in recruitment. A distinction is made between deterministic automation, algorithmic systems, machine learning, and generative AI, which makes it possible to avoid equating any digital HR tool with artificial intelligence. Based on a systematized review of recent academic literature, comparative and content analysis, as well as analysis of regulatory documents, the evidence regarding the impact of AI on recruitment performance is synthesized. It is shown that the strongest evidence concerns operational effects: the ability to process large volumes of applications, automate repetitive tasks, support sourcing, screening, matching, and communication, and reduce recruiters’ workload. At the same time, the evidence is substantially less conclusive with respect to quality of hire, candidate experience, and the elimination of bias. The article analyzes algorithmic bias, indirect discrimination, opacity, false exclusion of qualified candidates, privacy and information-security risks, automation bias, and the potential dehumanization of recruitment. Particular attention is paid to meaningful human oversight and to the current regulatory framework, including the EU AI Act, the GDPR, and Ukrainian legislation. An author-developed matrix for assessing the appropriateness of AI use in recruitment is proposed. It combines the expected effect, strength of evidence, discrimination and privacy risks, severity of potential error, and the required level of human oversight. Three modes of AI use are substantiated: automation-preferred, AI-assisted decision-making, and human-led decision-making. The principle of proportionality between automation and risk is formulated, according to which the permissible autonomy of an AI system should decrease as the potential harm of an algorithmic outcome increases.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE INTEGRATION AND ACADEMIC PERFORMANCE IN PHILIPPINE SECONDARY EDUCATION: A MIXED-METHODS STUDY OF ICT LITERACY AND CLASSROOM CHALLENGES
items.abstract: This study examined artificial intelligence (AI) utilization, associated classroom challenges, and academic performance among Senior High School students at Tigao National High School, Surigao del Sur, Philippines, during the Academic Year 2025-2026. Employing a mixed-methods research design, the study involved 122 respondents comprising 107 students and 15 teachers. Quantitative data were gathered through questionnaires and pretest–posttest assessments and analyzed using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and paired-samples t-tests, while qualitative data were examined through thematic analysis. Findings revealed that respondents demonstrated functional ICT literacy (M = 3.72) and frequently utilized AI for research, writing assistance, and academic activities. Academic performance increased from a pretest mean percentage score of 60.76% to 65.42% in written assessments and 79.53% in oral assessments, with statistically significant differences (p < .05). ICT literacy demonstrated a significant positive relationship with academic performance (r = .52, p < .05). Qualitative findings identified unreliable internet connectivity, limited devices, academic integrity concerns, and excessive AI dependence as persistent challenges. The study concluded that responsible AI integration, strengthened digital literacy, and appropriate instructional safeguards are essential to supporting academic achievement and equitable technology-enhanced learning.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy and Public Acceptance of AI Technologies among Adults in Iraq
items.abstract: This study investigated the relationship between Artificial Intelligence (AI) literacy and public acceptance of AI technologies among adults in Iraq. The role of AI in public services, healthcare, education, banking, and digital communication is growing, making it a key sociological and policy issue to understand what factors affect citizens' acceptance of AI. A quantitative cross sectional survey design was used and data were gathered from 420 adults living in Iraq. Artificial Intelligence literacy and public acceptance of AI technologies were measured by a structured questionnaire with a five-point Likert scale. The data were analysed by descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, exploratory factor analysis, Pearson correlation and regression analysis using IBM SPSS Statistics software. The results showed that the participants had a moderate to high level of AI literacy and moderate levels of public acceptance of AI technologies. The Pearson correlation analysis showed that there was a statistically significant positive correlation between the concepts of artificial intelligence literacy and public acceptance. The regression analysis also revealed that AI literacy was a significant predictor of public acceptance, accounting for 32.0% of the variance, and multiple regression analysis indicated that AI literacy is the most significant predictor, even after controlling for demographic and technology-related characteristics. The study is a significant contribution to the sociology of artificial intelligence, as it illustrates how AI literacy is a crucial social resource that influences citizens' receptivity to new technologies. The results highlight the need to encourage AI literacy initiatives to foster informed public acceptance and facilitate responsible digital transformation in Iraq.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-enabled updating and application of guideline-based algorithms for symptom management in adults with cancer: a concordance evaluation of cancer-related fatigue, depression, and pain
items.abstract: Introduction Cancer-related fatigue, depression, and pain are highly prevalent, often co-occur and impair physical function, social activities, and quality of life among adults with cancer. Despite the availability of evidence-based clinical guidelines that provide recommendations for assessment and management, these symptoms remain under-recognized and undertreated. Clinical decision support systems (CDSS) can operationalize guideline-based symptom management algorithms at the point of care. However, maintaining these systems as evidence and practice evolve is labor-intensive, limiting adoption and sustainability. To address this gap, we sought to evaluate an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled approach to updating guideline-based algorithms and generating patient-specific recommendations for managing fatigue, depression, and pain among adults with cancer. Methods This study evaluated AI performance (Gemini 3.0 Pro) for two tasks: identifying and interpreting updates to cancer symptom management guidelines for fatigue, depression, and pain, and producing casespecific recommendations aligned with an existing rule-based CDSS. Guideline updates were assessed against expert-judged reference standards using an ordinal rubric for detection, completeness, accuracy, and safety. Vignette-based recommendations were compared using precision, recall, and F1-score at the level of discrete clinical recommendation elements. Results For guideline updating, AI performance met pre-specified acceptability thresholds for fatigue and pain, with high completeness and accuracy and no clinical safety risk. Performance for depression was variable, driven by omission of guideline-supported integrative therapies and non-specific pharmacotherapy guidance. In vignette analyses, AI-generated recommendations showed strong concordance with the rule-based CDSS (F1 0.86–0.96). items.title: Assessing individual differences in teachers' proactive behavior: insights into the reliability and stability of high and low inference measures
items.abstract: Despite growing interest in teachers as agents of change, research lacks a coherent framework for studying teachers' initiatives to improve their school environments. Drawing on research in organizational psychology, the present study investigates two complementary measurement approaches to assess teachers' proactive behavior, defined as self-initiated actions to enhance school functioning and facilitate organizational improvement: first, teaching-specific adaptations of three established high-inference scales intended to capture different types of proactive behavior (voice, taking charge, and personal initiative), and second, a newly developed low-inference behavior checklist. Using two samples of German teachers ( N EarlyCareerSample = 165, N Cross − AgeSample = 130), we demonstrate that the instruments assess proactive behavior reliably, are substantially interrelated, and show the expected associations with the established constructs organizational citizenship behavior and work engagement. Evidence for the distinctiveness of voice, taking charge, and personal initiative was stronger in the Early Career Sample than in the Cross-Age Sample, where the dimensions showed considerable overlap. The behavior checklist captures a broad range of concrete proactive actions and is strongly related to all three high-inference measures. Beyond introducing instruments for assessing proactive behavior in teachers, the findings reveal meaningful variation across teachers, schools, and over time, support the empirical distinctiveness of proactive behavior from organizational citizenship behavior, and demonstrate its positive association with work engagement.

items.title: Assessing the safety and vulnerability of educational systems against disaster risks using the SAVES tool
items.abstract: Extreme weather and climate events impacted schools serving approximately 242 million students in 85 countries in 2024. Despite growing recognition of schools’ role in disaster risk management, the literature lacks integrated methods to assess schools’ exposure to water-related hazards, school building conditions, and the organizational capacities of educational systems to ensure school safety in the face of extreme events. This article proposes a tool for analyzing educational systems’ exposure, safety, and vulnerability to flood and landslide disasters across three spatial levels: river basin, municipal, and school unit. Based on the global vulnerability approach and UNESCO’s Comprehensive School Safety principles, the SAVES (Safety and Vulnerability of Educational Systems) tool proposes a hybrid index integrating school building conditions and organizational capacities. The index comprises three analytical dimensions with 34 indicators: (i) basic services dimension (BSD), measuring schools’ access to essential infrastructure; (ii) accessibility resources dimension (ARD), assessing physical accessibility features; and (iii) human resources dimension (HRD), evaluating organizational capacities through available personnel. The tool assessed schools’ exposure to floods and landslides in three municipalities within the Paraíba do Sul River Basin, Brazil. Results show that although schools have sufficient human resources to maintain daily operations, they face significant limitations in the availability of strategic professionals needed to ensure school safety during crises. Approximately 62% (n = 3,888) of schools lack accessible classrooms, revealing significant gaps in inclusive safety preparedness. Across all municipalities, many schools near risk areas showed particularly low ARD and HRD values, compounding these vulnerabilities.

items.title: Beyond “She’ll be right”: Building the Habit of Health for the Next Generation of Workplace Health
items.abstract: What if the very people responsible for protecting workplace health and safety are unintentionally standing in the way of support? WorkSafe New Zealand's 2025 Workforce Insights Programme, surveying 1,643 employers and 1,824 workers, revealed a concerning disconnect. While 88% of employers believed health and safety risks were discussed openly and helpfully, only 64% of workers agreed. This 24-percentage-point perception gap raises an uncomfortable question for health and safety professionals: Are we opening pathways to support, or becoming the gatekeepers who prevent people from accessing it? With five generations in New Zealand's workforce and increasing cultural diversity, workers communicate concerns and seek support differently. Complex reporting processes, delayed responses and assumptions about what workers need can discourage early help-seeking, allowing injuries, burnout and psychosocial risks to escalate. Drawing on Habit Health's experience in occupational health, injury management, rehabilitation and Employee Assistance Programme (EAP) services, the presentation highlights the value of early intervention. Habit Health's rehabilitation programme reported reductions in average compensation days from 147 to 56, average claim costs from $23,500 to $14,100, and return-to-work time from 238 to 118 days, alongside patient satisfaction of 9.6/10. Drawing from the success of the program while challenging traditional approaches, I introduce the G.A.T.E. framework. Through this I am encouraging health and safety professionals to: G: Give permission to speak up. A: Ask and act early when warning signs emerge. T: Tailor pathways to individual needs. E: Evidence the response and demonstrate tangible improvements. Through timely clinical intervention, accessible counselling, workplace rehabilitation and proactive occupational health support, Habit Health demonstrates how organisations can turn early warning signs into meaningful action. Every health and safety professional influences the gate. The question is whether your actions are helping people walk through it.

items.title: Beyond Operational Fluency: A Three-Tier AI Literacy Architecture for Reskilling and Upskilling in Strategic Talent Development
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) occupies two positions in talent development simultaneously: the principal driver of the reskilling imperative, obsoleting skills faster than organizations can replace them, and increasingly the instrument through which reskilling is delivered, via adaptive platforms, generated content, and automated coaching. Reskilling scholarship assumes training technology is causally independent of the skill shift it responds to, an assumption prior industrial transitions permitted but AI's shared mechanism no longer does. This conceptual paper argues that AI's dual position generates five failure modes conventional reskilling models cannot detect: velocity without capability, a deskilling loop in which the instrument reproduces the condition it was deployed to remedy, personalization that fragments collective capability, stratified access that widens the divide reskilling was meant to close, and erosion of the entry-level roles through which experiential learning occurs. Drawing on integrative reviews of AI and workers' skills, Industry 4.0 reskilling blueprints, and AI governance scholarship, the paper applies the HUMAN framework (Human Oversight, Upskilling for AI Literacy, Meaningful Augmentation, Accountability and Audit, Networked Learning) to each failure mode, and extends its upskilling principle into a three-tier AI literacy architecture, operational fluency, evaluative literacy, and complementary capability, that depreciates at rates inverse to the investment it typically attracts. The paper translates this into five testable propositions and offers implementation guidance differentiated by organizational context.

items.title: BEYOND PERSONALIZATION: METACOGNITIVE AI SCAFFOLDING FOR MULTILINGUAL LEARNERS OF ENGLISH IN INDIA
items.abstract: Integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into English language education has created new opportunitiesfor personalised, adaptive, and learner-centred instruction. However, multilingual learners in Indiaencounter distinctive challenges arising from linguistic diversity, unequal language proficiency,mother-tongue interference, and differences in educational backgrounds. Although conventional AIpowered personalisation provides individualised content and feedback, it often prioritises immediateperformance improvement rather than developing learners’ awareness of their own learning processes.To address this limitation, the present study proposes Metacognitive AI Scaffolding as an innovativepedagogical approach that moves beyond personalisation toward conscious, reflective, and selfregulated English language learning. The study examines how AI-based scaffolding can supportmultilingual learners in planning, monitoring, evaluating, and regulating their language-learningstrategies. Using a qualitative, conceptual research methodology, the study draws on existing literatureon artificial intelligence in education, metacognition, scaffolding, multilingual pedagogy, and selfregulated learning. It explores the potential of AI tools to provide reflective prompts, diagnosticfeedback, guided questioning, and adaptive learning support while recognising learners’ multilingualbackgrounds. The proposed framework seeks to reposition AI from a content-delivery mechanism toa metacognitive learning partner. Ultimately, the study contributes to an inclusive and learner-centredframework for English language education in India by strengthening learner autonomy, criticalreflection, and multilingual competence.

items.title: Beyond the tool: a systematic realist synthesis of cognitive agency in human-GenAI interaction in higher education
items.abstract: Cognitive agency concerns learners’ effortful, self-directed control over reasoning with generative AI (GenAI). Building on an existing implementation-level classification of generative AI use, this review examines how cognitive work is allocated between learners and AI tools. Following PRISMA 2020, searches of Scopus and Web of Science (2021–2025) yielded 93 peer-reviewed studies, appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. A realist synthesis specified an a priori program theory crossing the type of work offloaded (extraneous versus germane; cognitive load theory) with processing of AI output (heuristic acceptance versus analytical scrutiny; dual-process theory), and audited the evidence on each axis under manifest coding (reported evidence only) and latent coding (adding design-based inference). Under manifest coding, 21 studies were located on both axes; all four configurations occurred, two in a single study each, and the nine Cognitive Extension studies reported peripheral uses with analytical scrutiny. Of the 93 studies, 49 reported no learner behavior toward AI output, 69 reported no learning measure independent of AI assistance, and four reported processing evidence together with such a measure. Group differences or part-sample outcomes were documented in 30 studies; one further study reported stage differences, but no learner-, task-, or assessment-level moderator showed an interpretable corpus-level association with substitution. This evidence profile identifies the process and AI-independent learning measures needed to distinguish cognitive extension from cognitive substitution. The review restates the Heterogeneous Pathways of Distributed Agency (HPDA) Model as seven testable propositions and specifies the process-tracing and AI-independent outcome designs needed to test them.

items.title: Beyond the tool: what a course-aligned AI assistant reveals about student learning in microbiology
items.abstract: Course-aligned artificial intelligence (AI) tutors are increasingly offered as learning support in higher education. Beyond providing practice and feedback, they may also help teachers identify gaps in understanding across a cohort. In a second-year medical microbiology and immunology unit of 500 to 800 students, a course-aligned AI assistant built on The University of Sydney’s Cogniti platform gave students scenario-based short-answer practice with rubric-referenced feedback. Its conversation logs turned out to be a diagnostic instrument. Across more than 1300 conversations, the logs revealed cohort-level knowledge gaps and recurring terminology errors mid-semester. An exploratory analysis also found small positive correlations between practice-oriented use of the assistant and final short-answer marks, although these findings should be interpreted cautiously. The gaps were fed back to the class through an interactive revision resource used in lectures. These insights could be obtained through three approaches requiring different levels of technical expertise: the platform’s own no-code summaries, method-led coding with basic programming, and specialist computational analysis. We also discuss how the approach can be adapted where no equivalent platform exists. The project highlights that a course-aligned AI assistant can provide valuable insight into cohort-level understanding of the subject.
